articles.title: Giant robotic claws will grab dead satellites in space
articles.summary: ClearSpace UK's robotic spacecraft with giant claws will chase down dead satellites at 17,000 mph, with a 2029 launch from Scotland planned.
articles.body: Space is getting crowded, and I'm not talking about astronauts. Thousands of pieces of junk are circling Earth at incredible speeds. Some are dead satellites. Others are leftover rocket parts or fragments from past collisions. Any one of them could cause serious trouble if it hits a working spacecraft. Now Britain has a pretty wild solution. It's developing a robotic spacecraft with giant claws that can grab dead satellites and move them toward a fiery end in Earth's atmosphere. Think of a garbage truck in orbit, except this one has to track down its trash while both objects are traveling thousands of miles per hour. The UK is putting roughly $81 million behind the project. And if everything goes according to plan, the mission could change how we deal with the growing mess above our heads. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. WILL A FOUR-ARMED ROBOT REPLACE ASTRONAUTS IN SPACE? Britain's $81 million plan to clean up space The UK Space Agency has selected aerospace company ClearSpace UK to develop a spacecraft specifically designed to remove dead satellites from orbit. The contract is valued at approximately $81 million. The project is part of Britain's Active Debris Removal mission, known as UK ADR. The spacecraft is targeted for launch in 2029 from SaxaVord Spaceport in Scotland's Shetland Islands. Its first job will be to remove two defunct UK-registered satellites from low Earth orbit. The government wants both satellites removed by 2032. If successful, the mission would demonstrate that one spacecraft can capture and dispose of multiple dead satellites without being sacrificed after its first cleanup. That could make future operations far more practical, especially as the number of satellites in orbit continues to grow. How giant robotic claws will grab dead satellites Catching a satellite sounds straightforward until you consider what's happening in orbit. Objects in low Earth orbit typically travel at roughly 17,000 mph or faster. Some dead satellites may also tumble, making them difficult to approach safely. That's where ClearSpace's robotic technology comes in. The spacecraft will use a specialized capture system to approach and secure an inactive satellite. First, it must carefully coordinate its movements with the target. Then its robotic capture mechanism will take hold of the object. Once the satellite is secured, the spacecraft will move it into a lower orbit and release it. Atmospheric drag will eventually pull the abandoned satellite down, causing it to reenter Earth's atmosphere, where it is expected to burn up. The cleanup spacecraft itself is being designed for potential refueling and reuse. That means it could remain in orbit for future work instead of ending its mission after disposing of one satellite. Of course, engineers still have to prove the technology can handle these demanding operations safely. Why space junk is becoming a serious problem You might assume there's plenty of room in space for a few broken satellites. Unfortunately, some of the orbital regions where satellites operate are becoming increasingly crowded. According to the European Space Agency's space debris statistics, updated October 14, 2026, approximately 47,140 objects are regularly tracked in Earth's orbit. That figure includes functioning satellites, inactive spacecraft, rocket bodies and debris. And those are only the objects large enough to track reliably. ESA estimates that millions of smaller pieces also surround Earth. The danger comes from their enormous speeds. A piece of debris measuring just one centimeter can carry enough energy to disable a spacecraft. ESA has also warned that an impact of that size could penetrate the protective shielding of the International Space Station. Now consider what happens when two large objects collide. They can break apart and produce many additional fragments, each capable of damaging something else. Scientists call this potential chain reaction the Kessler syndrome. If enough collisions occur, certain orbital regions could become extremely hazardous for future missions. ESA's 2026 Space Environment Report warns that active debris removal will be necessary to prevent long-term debris growth driven by collisions. TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY Space junk also threatens astronauts The danger extends beyond expensive satellites. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station face risks from debris traveling through orbit. In November 2021, crew members took shelter inside their spacecraft after a Russian anti-satellite weapons test created a dangerous cloud of debris. NASA confirmed that astronauts and cosmonauts closed hatches and sheltered inside docked Dragon and Soyuz spacecraft while teams evaluated the threat. Fortunately, the station and crew remained safe. The incident demonstrated how quickly debris from a satellite breakup can disrupt operations in orbit. A serious impact could damage critical systems or puncture a spacecraft's pressurized structure. That's why space agencies continuously monitor debris and sometimes adjust spacecraft orbits to avoid potential collisions. Removing larger abandoned satellites could help prevent future collisions that create even more fragments. Could space junk fall back to Earth? Here's another concern that deserves attention. Some space debris eventually returns to Earth, and certain components can survive the intense heat of atmospheric reentry. Most smaller debris burns up. However, larger objects and components made from heat-resistant materials can sometimes reach the ground. As rocket launches increase, researchers are paying closer attention to this danger. Space environmentalist Ewan Wright, from the University of British Columbia, told Space.com that approximately 124 rocket stages reentered Earth's atmosphere uncontrolled in 2024. He estimated that if that annual level continued for a decade, there would be a 33% probability of at least one person somewhere in the world being killed by falling rocket debris. That estimate describes a cumulative global risk from rocket stages, rather than the danger posed by Britain's two satellite-removal targets. ESA also reports that the risk of casualties from uncontrolled reentries has increased in recent years, although the overall probability remains low compared with many everyday risks. The takeaway here is that removing debris from orbit requires careful planning. Operators must consider what happens when that material eventually returns to Earth. A new space cleanup industry could be taking shape Britain's mission could have implications well beyond the two satellites it plans to remove. For years, many satellites were designed primarily to complete their missions and then be retired. Some remain in orbit long after they stop functioning. Now companies are developing spacecraft capable of approaching other satellites and performing tasks that once seemed incredibly difficult. ClearSpace's mission could help prove that robotic spacecraft can safely capture objects that were never designed for servicing. Its planned refueling capability is particularly interesting. Instead of launching a new cleanup vehicle for every job, operators could eventually service an existing spacecraft and send it after more debris. That could open the door to a new commercial industry. Satellite operators might eventually pay specialized companies to remove aging equipment or extend the useful lives of working spacecraft. However, the UK mission remains in development. Its long-term commercial potential will depend on whether the technology performs as expected. What this means to you You probably don't spend much time thinking about abandoned satellites while checking the weather or following GPS directions. But the technology operating above Earth plays an enormous role in everyday life. Satellites support communication networks, provide navigation signals and deliver information used for weather forecasting. They also help scientists monitor changes on Earth and support emergency response operations. GPS satellites operate in medium Earth orbit, much higher than the low Earth orbit debris targeted by Britain's mission. Still, the broader effort to keep orbital regions safer helps protect the infrastructure that supports satellite-based services. A collision that disables an important spacecraft could disrupt operations and force companies or government agencies to rely on backup systems. Replacing a damaged satellite can also be expensive. Britain's robotic cleanup mission won't eliminate the space junk problem overnight. But successfully removing two abandoned satellites could help establish a practical way to deal with dangerous objects already in orbit. And with thousands of additional satellites being launched, finding a reliable way to retire them safely could become increasingly important. Kurt's key takeaways I have to admit, the idea of a spacecraft chasing down dead satellites with giant robotic claws sounds like something Hollywood dreamed up. But I find the technology fascinating, especially when you consider how much we depend on satellites without giving them a second thought. What really caught my attention is the possibility of reusing the cleanup spacecraft. That could make removing space junk a routine service rather than an occasional experiment. Still, I wonder whether we're moving fast enough. With companies launching more satellites every year, cleaning up two abandoned spacecraft feels like a small start. I'd like to see satellite operators take greater responsibility for what they leave behind. After all, we wouldn't tolerate companies abandoning broken equipment on our highways. Why should Earth's orbit be any different? articles.title: ‘Real consequences’: AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile warn FCC as Elon Musk plots a SpaceX phone network for the US by 2028
articles.summary: AT&T and T-Mobile stock sank nearly 8% after a report that SpaceX wants 80,000 cell sites. Here’s what the carriers asked the FCC, and what it could mean for...
articles.body:
AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile have spent months insisting a satellite company can't compete with their networks. Investors aren't convinced.

On Oct. 23, shares of AT&T (NYSE:T) and T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS) each fell nearly 8% after Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is in talks to access at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites, a step toward becoming the country's fourth nationwide carrier. Verizon (NYSE:VZ) slipped about 1.2%.

The selloff came a day after the carriers' trade group, CTIA, filed a letter with the Federal Communications Commission following Oct. 20 meetings with agency officials. In it, CTIA warned that "the Commission's buildout decisions have real consequences for consumers who rely on ever-increasing wireless capacity to access the modern economy and support their day-to-day living."

The letter doesn't mention SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX), which wants to become one of those carriers. On the company's Oct. 20 earnings call , President Gwynne Shotwell said a new spectrum purchase and the FCC's approval of its next satellites would "pave the way" for Starlink Mobile to become a major U.S. mobile carrier, with service on its own airwaves targeted for early 2028. Musk told analysts he sees "a clear path to several hundred billion dollars a year" in connectivity revenue, from a business that brought in about $5.2 billion in the third quarter.

The U.S. hasn't had four national carriers since T-Mobile bought Sprint in 2020. Regulators approved the deal expecting Dish Network to build a fourth network. The plan fell apart in 2025, when Dish's parent, EchoStar, agreed to sell spectrum to AT&T for about $23 billion and to SpaceX in deals now worth about $19.6 billion, and moved its Boost Mobile customers onto AT&T's network. The FCC approved AT&T's purchase and SpaceX's in May.

That's when a satellite beams a signal straight to an ordinary phone using airwaves licensed to a regular carrier.

articles.title: How Trump learned to stop worrying and love space science
articles.summary: He recognizes a cool thing when he sees it.
articles.body:
Ars Technica has reported that two NASA Venus probes have escaped the Trump White House budget axe. The development represents a subtle and welcome development concerning the administration’s attitude toward science missions that are not directly related to the Artemis return to the moon program.

The Deep Atmosphere Venus Investigation of Noble gases, Chemistry, and Imaging, or DAVINCI, mission will take off a year earlier than previously scheduled in December 2030. It will launch “a parachute-assisted descent probe through Venus’ atmosphere, returning the first direct images of the planet’s surface since 1982.”

The Venus Emissivity, Radio science, InSAR, Topography, And Spectroscopy, or VERITAS, mission “will follow with a launch in November 2032 to map the Venusian surface by radar from orbit.”

The greenlighting of two Venus missions is remarkable. As recently as April, the Trump administration proposed cutting NASA science , which includes the Venus probes, by roughly half. Everything outside Artemis was in jeopardy of the chopping block to help address the massive budget deficits the United States government is facing

Part of the reason that DAVINCI and VERITAS are going forward is that Congress, just as in 2025, is balking at the proposed cuts to NASA science missions. Another part is that some of the cuts were found by cancelling the Mars Sample Return mission , which was suffering from cost overruns and schedule delays.

The situation NASA finds itself in is nothing new. The historical record suggests that during the early days of the Apollo race to the moon, President John F. Kennedy was entirely uninterested in space exploration in and of itself. He saw the Apollo program as an instrument of the Cold War, a way to demonstrate the superiority of the United States over the Soviet Union.

Kennedy’s attitude was a source of endless frustration to his NASA administrator , James Webb, who wanted to fund missions outside of Apollo, such as the Mariner probes to Venus and Mars.

However, some evidence exists that President Trump is beginning to appreciate NASA science missions that are not part of Artemis. In August, when NASA launched the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from the Kennedy Launch Center on top of a SpaceX Falcon Heavy, President Trump praised the mission with a post on Truth Social.

“Congratulations to NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and the Great Patriots at NASA, on a successful launch. This is THE GOLDEN AGE OF AMERICA!”

Trump also called into the post-launch press conference to offer more fulsome praise for NASA on the successful launch.

Ironically, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope had been in danger of cancellation because of the proposed White House budget cuts. So, why the sudden change of heart?

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is an impressive undertaking, like the James Webb and the Hubble space telescopes. It will hunt for exoplanets, delve into the mysteries of dark energy and perform a great deal of other infrared astronomy. President Trump is quite right to celebrate its launch, as it will expand the frontiers of our knowledge of the universe. He recognizes a cool thing when he sees it.

On the other hand, Trump is a practical politician who knows how to make the best out of a policy reverse. The president, seeing what the political zeitgeist is, has become a champion of space science as well as the Artemis program.

Even so, the $2 trillion a year budget deficit and the over $40 trillion national debt is still out there and needs to be fixed. But it looks like the federal government will have to look elsewhere than NASA to find some savings.

Space exploration has entered a unique period of history. The hugely expensive and ambitious undertaking of sending astronauts beyond low Earth orbit to the moon, Mars and beyond has gained popularity on both sides of the political divide. But so have other missions, including probes to Venus and space telescopes.

Historians will figure out why this new space age has come to be. Factors like the threat of China, the rise of space barons like Elon Musk, and charismatic and politically savvy NASA leaders such as Jared Isaacman and Jim Bridenstine all have come into play.

The world can be a frightful place, as anyone who has turned on a television or seen social media can attest. But, beyond the Earth something glorious and good is taking shape. There is hope for humanity yet.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well as “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.

articles.title: Arctic ice had been expanding for at least 1,000 years before reaching its greatest extent around 1960; researchers say greenhouse warming then reversed a natural slide toward another ice age
articles.summary: A new study suggests that the Arctic was already moving towards another glaciation nearly 2,000 years ago, before rising greenhouse gas emissions reversed
articles.body: A new study suggests that the Arctic was already moving towards another glaciation nearly 2,000 years ago, before rising greenhouse gas emissions reversed the trend. Researchers found that the Barnes Ice Cap in Canada's Arctic began expanding again around that time, reaching its greatest extent in this advance around 1960. It has since retreated, reversing centuries of ice growth.Published in Science on 22 October, the study, titled Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, examines the last surviving remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, which once covered much of Canada and parts of the northern United States. The researchers argue that human-caused global warming overwhelmed the natural cooling influence of changes in Earth's orbit, halting the ice cap's expansion. The findings offer physical evidence of a renewed glacial advance in the Arctic.How the Arctic ice cap began growing againThe Barnes Ice Cap, located on Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, covers an area roughly the size of Delaware. It is the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, which reached across much of North America during the last glacial period.According to the study's reconstruction, the ice cap reached its minimum interglacial dimensions around 3,600 years ago. It began expanding again approximately 2,000 years ago, as cooler summers allowed more snow and ice to survive the melting season. The advance continued for centuries, reaching its greatest extent around 1960.The trend then reversed. Since the 1980s, the ice cap's margins have retreated by an average of about four metres a year, according to reporting on the study. The researchers attribute this reversal to rising greenhouse gas emissions, which have warmed Arctic summers and caused the ice cap to lose more ice than it gains.The study's central argument is that this was not simply a local fluctuation in a glacier's size. The authors interpret the renewed expansion as the beginning of the next glaciation, interrupted before a much larger continental ice sheet could develop.What drives an ice age?The climate of the Earth naturally oscillates between colder glacial periods and warmer interglacial periods. We are now in the Holocene , a relatively warm period that began about 11,700 years ago , after the last glacial period .These long-term changes are driven by variations in Earth's orbit and orientation, known as Milankovitch cycles. They alter how sunlight is distributed across the planet, including how much summer sunlight reaches high northern latitudes.Cooler summers allow more snow to survive from one year to the next. Over long periods, this snow can accumulate into ice. As ice spreads, it reflects more sunlight back into space, encouraging further cooling and potentially allowing ice sheets to grow.The researchers argue that these natural conditions were favouring renewed ice growth while human-produced greenhouse gases increasingly warmed the atmosphere. By the 1960s, they say, the warming influence had become strong enough to reverse the advance.How researchers reconstructed the ice cap's historyThe evidence comes partly from plants preserved beneath the advancing ice. Because the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to its bedrock, rather than sliding over it like many glaciers, it can preserve vegetation that once grew on the exposed ground.As the ice advances, it covers and kills mosses and other plants. When the ice later retreats, these remains become exposed again. Researchers can use radiocarbon dating to estimate when the plants died, providing what scientists call a “kill date” for the advancing ice.By comparing dates from different locations, the team reconstructed the sequence of the ice cap's expansion. The researchers also used beryllium-10 exposure dating, which measures how long rocks have been exposed to cosmic radiation, to help establish when the landscape was last uncovered by ice.Historical aerial photographs and mapped ice margins provided additional evidence of the ice cap's more recent retreat.Taken together, these records indicate that the ice cap had already begun to expand again well before the modern reversal.The timing of that reversal is attributed by the researchers to anthropogenic warming, but they say more research is required to understand the precise mechanisms behind glacial inception.What does this mean for the next ice age?The findings revisit a debate from the early 1970s, when scientists discussed the possibility of an approaching glaciation. A meeting at Brown University reportedly prompted a warning letter to US President Richard Nixon. Later media coverage of the discussion, alongside a period of cooler weather, was frequently cited by climate-change skeptics as evidence against global warming.The new research does not suggest that global warming is a myth. Instead, its authors argue that natural conditions may have been favouring renewed ice growth, only for human-caused warming to reverse the trend.There are, however, important limits to what the study establishes. Evidence from the Barnes Ice Cap provides a detailed record of one region, but does not independently demonstrate that a new continental-scale ice age had begun across the planet. Other researchers have called for comparisons with records from additional locations to better understand the wider pattern.Nor does the study establish precisely when the next glaciation would otherwise have developed, or whether future glacial cycles have been permanently prevented. Elevated greenhouse gas concentrations make such predictions more difficult.The researchers project that the Barnes Ice Cap could disappear within the next few centuries. If it does, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet will be gone.The study offers a striking illustration of how human-caused warming can alter a long-running natural climate process. But the broader claim that humanity stopped the next ice age remains an interpretation of the evidence, rather than proof that a global glaciation was already imminent.

articles.title: The SS United States is scheduled for sinking to become the world's largest artificial reef
articles.summary: (AP) — A historic ocean liner is a step closer to becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.Officials in Florida's Okaloosa County expect to sink the SS U...
articles.body:
DESTIN, Fla. (AP) — A historic ocean liner is a step closer to becoming the world's largest artificial reef .

Officials in Florida's Okaloosa County expect to sink the SS United States off the Gulf Coast during the second week of November. The exact dates could change because of weather.

The ship will be sunk about 22 nautical miles (41 kilometers) southwest of Destin.

"This is an exciting move forward to create a one-of-a-kind resource for the environment and for our tourism industry," county officials wrote in a news release.

The nearly 1,000-foot (305-meter) vessel shattered the trans-Atlantic speed record on its maiden voyage in 1952. Preservation groups tried to save the ship but were hindered by high costs.

Supporters hope that sinking the ship will make it a barnacle-encrusted star among more than 500 artificial reefs and a signature diving attraction, helping to generate millions of dollars a year in local tourism spending for scuba shops, charter fishing boats and hotels.

articles.title: Grok releases the first seven minutes of its AI-generated ‘Odyssey’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The footage looks okay, as long as you're not seeking artistry, inspiration, or human interest.
articles.body:
Three months after Elon Musk declared that Grok would release a full-length, “historically accurate” movie version of “The Odyssey,” Grok has published a whole seven minutes — what the company is now calling “Episode 1 of our Odyssey series.”

Musk had previously lashed out at Christopher Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” because Nolan cast nonwhite and transgender actors. And Nolan is, in many ways, a perfect foil for Musk — while SpaceX and Tesla CEO hypes up data centers in space and posts an unending stream of AI-generated content, Nolan has described himself as “a techno-skeptic ” and said that before AI, he’d never seen a technology “so completely rejected by the public.”

And while Nolan’s version of “The Odyssey” certainly used plenty of visual effects, it’s primarily a feat of practical filmmaking , with a shoot spanning six countries and a cast and crew of thousands. After its release in July, the film became an extraordinary box office success , selling out Imax screenings for months and becoming the likely front-runner at the next Academy Awards .

As for the Grok version of “The Odyssey” (created in collaboration with Wonder Studios and director Dev Walker), well, you can watch for yourself.

I’ll admit it’s not as spectacularly ugly as I’d expected, and certainly more impressive than other videos that Musk has posted recently. If I didn’t know better, there were moments when I might have thought these were real actors sailing across a real sea. And while I can’t speak to Grok’s historical accuracy, it does seem that all the characters come in a Musk-approved skin color, while the narrator uses a British accent that will sound familiar to anyone who’s played a fantasy video game or watched a generic Hollywood epic from the past 25 years.

What the footage really lacks is any sense of artistry, inspiration, or human interest. The backstory — delivered via the aforementioned voiceover — seems to go on forever, finally giving way to one bearded face after another, each shouting stilted lines that make Nolan’s dialogue sound like Shakespeare.

While a few individual shots might provide a reasonable simulacrum of reality, the whole thing feels completely airless, offering viewers no sense of momentum, no reason to care about anyone or anything on-screen. And where I had no trouble paying attention for the nearly three-hour runtime of Nolan’s “Odyssey,” I was listlessly checking how much I had left before the Grok version was even halfway through.

It’s hard to imagine being interested in another seven minutes of this, much less a full movie’s worth.

articles.standfirst: Daniel Dahis venceu o Eric and Wendy Schmidt Awards, prêmio das Academias Nacionais de Ciências, Engenharia e Medicina dos EUA para quem aproxima a ciência do público.
articles.summary: Daniel Dahis venceu o Eric and Wendy Schmidt Awards, prêmio das Academias Nacionais de Ciências, Engenharia e Medicina dos EUA para quem aproxima a ciência do público.
articles.body:
Daniel Dahis é pesquisador e fala sobre ciência nas redes sociais — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O engenheiro biomédico Daniel Dahis é o primeiro brasileiro a vencer o Eric and Wendy Schmidt Awards for Excellence in Science Communication, prêmio que as Academias Nacionais de Ciências, Engenharia e Medicina dos Estados Unidos (NASEM, na sigla em inglês) concedem a quem leva ciência para além dos muros da universidade. O resultado foi anunciado nesta segunda-feira (26).

A edição de 2026 reconhece 24 profissionais em oito categorias, que incluem pesquisadores, jornalistas e criadores de conteúdo em diferentes fases da carreira. Cada categoria tem um vencedor principal, que recebe US$ 40 mil, e outros dois reconhecidos, com US$ 20 mil cada.

Dahis venceu na categoria Research Scientist: Early Career, voltada a pesquisadores em início de carreira. O destaque é pela divulgação científica que faz em suas redes sociais, onde acumula mais de 750 mil seguidores com quem compartilha vídeos em que explica como funcionam vacinas, doenças, tratamentos e novas pesquisas.

O pesquisador, que hoje está nos Estados Unidos, mas produz seu conteúdo principalmente em português, se disse surpreso com a premiação. Ele conta que dedicou anos da vida à pesquisa — o que ainda faz hoje —, mas desde 2024 passou a falar de ciência nas redes sociais.

“Nunca imaginei que um dia receberia um reconhecimento internacional por levar esse conhecimento para fora dos laboratórios”, diz.

Para ele, o reconhecimento de instituições de prestígio a um pesquisador brasileiro marca a importância da produção científica e da comunicação sobre ciência no país.

Daniel Dahis é pesquisador e é o primeiro brasileiro a receber prêmio das Academias Nacionais de Ciências, Engenharia e Medicina dos Estados Unidos — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Da bancada do laboratório às redes sociais

Dahis se formou em engenharia na Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), onde descobriu a engenharia biomédica. Depois, fez mestrado e doutorado no Technion, instituto de tecnologia em Haifa, em Israel, com pesquisas em oncologia feitas em colaboração com a Escola de Medicina de Harvard.

Uma das frentes do doutorado foi o melanoma, um tipo de câncer de pele. Ele trabalhou em uma estratégia inédita de vacina personalizada, que combinava imunoterapia, nanopartículas e ultrassom focalizado.

O mesmo estudo usou adesivos com microagulhas para coletar biomarcadores, sinais biológicos que mostram como o organismo está reagindo. Com eles, é possível acompanhar a resposta ao tratamento quase em tempo real e de forma pouco invasiva. Os testes, ainda em fase pré-clínica, antes da etapa com humanos, indicaram potencial tanto para combater o tumor quanto para monitorar a reação do sistema imunológico.

Em outra pesquisa que esteve envolvido, ele pesquisou o uso do ultrassom para ajudar nanopartículas carregadas de medicamento a atravessar a barreira hematoencefálica, uma espécie de filtro que protege o cérebro, mas também impede a chegada de muitos remédios. Esse é um dos grandes obstáculos no tratamento de tumores cerebrais, como o glioblastoma.

Nos experimentos com animais, a técnica aumentou em até 3,6 vezes a concentração das nanopartículas no cérebro. As duas pesquisas foram publicadas em 2023, nas revistas científicas “Advanced Functional Materials” e “Advanced NanoBiomed Research”.

Na BioDevek, em Boston, liderou os testes pré-clínicos de um gel adesivo em spray, criado para proteger feridas no sistema digestivo após procedimentos de endoscopia, como a retirada de pólipos. Aplicado sobre o tecido lesionado, o material forma uma barreira protetora. Em testes com porcos, durou de 3 a 7 dias, o que pode favorecer a cicatrização e reduzir complicações como sangramentos. O estudo saiu em 2024 na revista “Advanced Materials”.

Ele conta que, durante uma visita ao laboratório onde trabalhava em 2024, ouviu que a história de um brasileiro fazendo ciência com Harvard poderia inspirar jovens que sonham com a carreira científica.

O que começou como iniciativa pessoal hoje alcança milhões de pessoas. Ele produz conteúdo para as redes sociais e tem uma newsletter em que fala de ciência.

Dahis vê as redes como o espaço em que muita gente procura respostas sobre alimentação, vacinas e tratamentos, e onde a desinformação circula com aparência convincente, às vezes propagada por profissionais de saúde.

Ele lembra que quem tenta corrigir essas distorções paga um preço. Uma pesquisa da revista Nature publicada em 2021 mostrou que cerca de 15% dos 321 cientistas ouvidos que haviam falado publicamente sobre a Covid relataram ter recebido ameaças de morte.

“Precisamos de cada vez mais pessoas com formação científica participando do debate público para fazer frente a esse movimento que coloca pessoas vulneráveis em risco. Recentemente, vi um vídeo em que alguém perguntava: ‘Por que os cientistas estão fingindo ser influenciadores?’. E pensei: talvez porque alguns influenciadores sem letramento científico estejam fingindo ser cientistas”, comenta.

Depois de anos desenvolvendo e testando tecnologias médicas em laboratório, hoje atua nos Estados Unidos como cientista de desenvolvimento clínico. Seu foco são tecnologias para monitorar pacientes internados e identificar cedo sinais de que o quadro está piorando.

Para Dahis, o prêmio também reconhece o valor da divulgação científica feita em português, e ele espera que a conquista inspire outros pesquisadores e comunicadores do país.

articles.title: A Burmese python was found guarding 20 eggs beneath a Florida sidewalk; the discovery raised fears that more invasive snakes could be nesting near homes
articles.summary: A patch of pavement in South Florida offered an unlikely hiding place for a Burmese python during the busiest part of the species’ nesting season.
articles.body: A patch of pavement in South Florida offered an unlikely hiding place for a Burmese python during the busiest part of the species’ nesting season. The snake was discovered beneath a sidewalk, where it was guarding 20 eggs, after a passer-by noticed movement under the concrete. The encounter drew attention to the places where the invasive reptiles can settle, including areas close to residential neighbourhoods. For wildlife contractors working across the region, such discoveries are part of a wider effort to contain a population that has spread through Florida’s waterways and surrounding habitats. The number of eggs also raised a familiar concern: a single female can produce far more offspring than this.Burmese python nest discovered beneath a Florida sidewalkThe python was spotted when a man walking nearby noticed something moving beneath the sidewalk. Closer inspection revealed the snake sheltering under the concrete, with a clutch of eggs nearby. Guillermo Tapanes, a contractor working with the South Florida Water Management District, became involved in the discovery.The location offered a reminder of how difficult it can be to predict where the reptiles will turn up. Burmese pythons are frequently associated with the canals and wetlands of South Florida, which provide routes through the landscape and access to prey. Yet the snake beneath the pavement had found shelter in a setting more commonly associated with people than wildlife.Tapanes described the encounter as an example of the species' ability to make use of different surroundings. Its presence beneath a sidewalk also brought the issue closer to home for residents who might assume that nesting activity is confined to remote stretches of the Everglades.20 eggs represent only part of a python's reproductive capacityAlthough a clutch of 20 eggs may appear substantial, it is relatively modest for a large female Burmese python. The snakes can produce dozens of eggs, with particularly large individuals capable of carrying or laying well over 100.Tapanes recalled other encounters involving females with considerably larger clutches. A python measuring about 14 feet was found with 53 eggs, while an individual measuring almost 18 feet had an estimated 200 eggs developing inside its body before laying. The latter case illustrated the potential reproductive capacity of a mature female, even before the eggs have been deposited in a nest.The number of eggs beneath the sidewalk therefore tells only part of the story. A single successful nesting event can add many young snakes to an established population. How many ultimately survive is another matter, but the scale of egg production helps explain why removing breeding females and their eggs is part of Florida's continuing control work.Why the timing of the discovery mattersThe snake was found during the peak of the Burmese python nesting season in South Florida. The eggs were not expected to hatch until early autumn, according to the report, leaving a period in which intervention could prevent that particular clutch from producing hatchlings.Finding nests is not always straightforward. A python may remain concealed while protecting its eggs, and suitable hiding places can occur in a range of environments. The discovery beneath a pavement surface illustrated how a nest might go unnoticed until somebody happens to see movement or encounters the animal.For contractors, the timing makes reports from members of the public particularly useful. Tapanes said that he had already captured 23 pythons during May and had caught more than 100 since beginning work as a contractor. His account reflected the continuing activity of teams attempting to remove the invasive snakes from the region.How Burmese pythons became established in FloridaThe species is native to South and Southeast Asia, rather than the wetlands of Florida. Its presence in the state is closely linked to the exotic pet trade, through which snakes were brought into the country. Some were subsequently released into the wild when owners could no longer manage them.Hurricane Andrew, which struck South Florida in 1992, is also part of the history of the invasion. Tapanes referred to a breeding facility in the Homestead area that was destroyed during the storm, allowing snakes to escape into the surrounding environment. The precise contribution of that event to the wider population is difficult to separate from other introductions, but it has become one of the commonly cited episodes in the species' establishment.Florida's warm, humid conditions provide a favourable environment for the reptiles. Over time, Burmese pythons have become established across parts of South Florida, particularly in and around the Everglades. Their ability to move through canals and waterways gives them access to extensive areas of suitable habitat.Consequences for native wildlife and household petsBurmese pythons are opportunistic predators. They consume a wide range of animals, and their presence in Florida has been associated with substantial declines in several native mammal populations in parts of the Everglades. Their diet can include mammals and birds, depending on the prey available.The risk can extend into residential areas, where domestic animals may also be vulnerable. Tapanes said pythons had been seen near neighbourhood lakes and warned that cats and dogs could become prey if a snake encountered them. That does not mean every sighting presents an immediate danger to a pet or person, but it does underline the importance of keeping animals under supervision in areas where pythons are known to occur.Florida requires captured Burmese pythons to be euthanised under its invasive-species rules. Tapanes said his work follows American Veterinary Medical Association standards for humane euthanasia. The policy reflects the state's aim of limiting the spread of a non-native predator that is difficult to eradicate once established.Residents urged to report sightingsMembers of the public can help wildlife officials locate snakes by reporting sightings rather than attempting to handle them. Florida's IveGot1 app provides a way to submit reports of invasive species, including Burmese pythons, so that the information can be passed to the relevant authorities.A sighting beneath a sidewalk may seem unusual, but the underlying issue is familiar to those involved in python removal. The animals can occupy unexpected spaces, and nesting females may remain hidden until somebody notices them. Reporting an encounter promptly can give trained personnel an opportunity to assess the situation and remove the snake or eggs where appropriate.

articles.title: University of Cambridge researchers develop a $10 spectrometer chip that identifies food, plastics and pharmaceuticals, with potential applications in wearable health monitoring
articles.summary: Researchers at the University of Cambridge have developed a compact optical spectrometer that costs around $10 and delivers laboratory-grade precision for
articles.body: Researchers at the University of Cambridge have developed a compact optical spectrometer that costs around $10 and delivers laboratory-grade precision for applications ranging from healthcare monitoring to food and materials analysis. The device was developed with GlitterinTech, a start-up founded by the same research group.According to the University of Cambridge's Department of Engineering, it uses a new type of spectrometer, called a convolutional spectrometer, to measure light. The chip operates across a near-infrared range of 1,200 to 1,700 nanometres and supports sub-second sampling and processing. Tests classified plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour and tea with a 100% success rate.How the $10 chip analyses light to identify materialsThe researchers developed a new class of optical spectrometer that uses the convolution theorem to retrieve spectra. Unlike conventional instruments that disperse light or rely on algorithmic reconstruction, this device physically performs a convolution operation on incoming light. It uses cascaded optical components with periodic spectral responses, including unbalanced Mach–Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators.Proportional tuning shifts the system's spectral response linearly, allowing the spectrum to be recovered using fast Fourier transforms. Dr Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study, said, “By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturised spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system”.The compact spectrometer maintains stability from -20°C to 80°CThe spectrometer was implemented on a silicon nitride photonic integration platform and packaged with on-board electronics. It operates across an ultra-wide near-infrared range of 1,200 to 1,700 nanometres, with sampling and processing times below one second. Its periodic design allows bandwidth expansion in the spectral domain without changing the hardware. Resolution can also be scaled exponentially by cascading additional components.These features address limitations associated with conventional miniaturised spectrometers, which often sacrifice bandwidth, resolution or accuracy as their size decreases. The researchers also demonstrated that the device remained stable across temperatures ranging from minus 20°C to 80°C, supporting its potential use in wearable, industrial and outdoor settings.Spectrometer chip classifies food, plastics and pharmaceuticals with high accuracyThe researchers tested the device on several materials and food products. It classified plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour and tea with a 100% success rate. It also measured concentrations in aqueous and organic solutions with accuracies of around 0.01%, outperforming commercial benchtop spectrometers. These results demonstrated its potential for materials analysis, food testing and industrial quality control.The team designed the system to recover spectral information with minimal computational processing. Conventional high-performance miniaturised spectrometers often require complex calibration procedures and computationally intensive reconstruction algorithms that can be sensitive to noise.By contrast, the convolutional approach supports fast and stable spectrum recovery, making the compact device suitable for applications requiring precise measurements.Non-invasive glucose monitoring expands the chip's healthcare applicationsThe spectrometer also demonstrated non-invasive sensing of human biomarkers under realistic physiological conditions. Tests measured skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose with high accuracy. The researchers demonstrated glucose tracking over extended periods in a single participant.Project leader Professor Qixiang Cheng said, “These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting”.“What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr Chunhui Yao’s contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment.”

articles.title: El barco eléctrico más grande del mundo empieza a transportar pasajeros: capacidad para 2.100 personas y 225 vehículos
articles.standfirst: La Embarcación de 130 metros construida en Australia lleva personas entre Argentina y Uruguay
articles.summary: La Embarcación de 130 metros construida en Australia lleva personas entre Argentina y Uruguay
articles.body: Las características del barco eléctrico más grande del mundo ya han llamado la atención. Lo hicieron con anterioridad a llevar pasajeros, simplemente por su tamaño, que son unos 130 metros. Está construido en Australia y en los últimos días ha dado un importante paso: ya es capaz de transportar personas, tal y como se ha podido comprobar recientemente. Su capacidad ha quedado demostrada: para 2.100 personas y 225 vehículos, que incluyen coches y también autobuses. El recorrido, por ahora, une Argentina con Uruguay, en Sudamérica. El pasado viernes, Incat Tasmania, la empresa encargada de la fabricación de la embarcación eléctrica más grande del mundo, anunció este hito histórico. Fue el primer viaje comercial entre Buenos Aires y Colonia. Lo ha hecho después de semanas y meses de pruebas. De hecho, empezaron hace prácticamente un año, en 2025. Fue en ese momento cuando se puso en funcionamiento con pruebas portuarias en el río Derwent, en Tasmania. Esa fue la primera vez que se propulsó eléctricamente a batería. Lógicamente, se ha convertido en un hito histórico. Ya no solo para la empresa o para los constructores. También lo ha sido para el sector marítimo mundial. Así al menos lo ha considerado Robert Clifford, presidente de Incat. “Durante años, cientos de personas con talento en nuestro astillero de Hobart han trabajado sin descanso para dar vida a esta extraordinaria embarcación. Hemos superado enormes retos técnicos, hemos ampliado los límites de lo que se creía posible y hemos construido algo que el mundo nunca había visto antes”, ha celebrado. “Ver ahora cómo este barco transporta pasajeros en servicio comercial, propulsado íntegramente por baterías, es un logro increíble y un motivo de enorme orgullo para todos los que han formado parte de este viaje”, ha añadido en declaraciones que recoge el portal web The Driven.

articles.title: Meet Violet Clinton: 16-year-old New York student who tracked 11,377 moths in seven months using UV lights and beer-soaked T-shirts to study overlooked pollinators
articles.summary: At 16, Violet Clinton has turned her fascination with insects into an ambitious scientific research project, documenting 11,377 insects during a
articles.body: At 16, Violet Clinton has turned her fascination with insects into an ambitious scientific research project, documenting 11,377 insects during a seven-month study of moth diversity and abundance in New York. A student at Horace Greeley High School, she spends two or three evenings a week exploring the Eugene and Agnes Meyer Nature Preserve in Armonk, using ultraviolet lights, a butterfly net and homemade bait made from bananas, brown sugar and beer to attract moths. Her research examines three habitats under different weather conditions and moon phases. The project has also earned her recognition at a scientific competition, where she secured second place among college and graduate student researchers, according to a report by The New York Times.How Violet Clinton tracked 11,377 moths in seven monthsClinton's interest in insects began during childhood, when she regularly searched for grasshoppers and other small creatures. One of her earliest memorable encounters with moths occurred when she was about seven and brought home two woolly bear caterpillars she had found crawling along a pavement.During winter, she thought the caterpillars had died. When spring arrived, they emerged as Isabella tiger moths with distinctive orange wings. The experience deepened her curiosity about insects and their life cycles.By the summer between middle school and high school, Clinton was studying insect field guides to prepare for entomology competitions as part of her school's Science Olympiad team. Her family supported her interest, allowing her to raise hornworms bought from a pet shop until they developed into Carolina sphinx moths.Her fascination eventually became a formal research project. At the beginning of her sophomore year, a science research course at Horace Greeley High School required students to choose a subject to investigate. While some students opted to analyse existing datasets, Clinton decided to conduct her own fieldwork.She contacted Jason J. Dombroskie, an entomologist who manages the Cornell University Insect Collection, seeking guidance on developing her project. They began meeting online in January to refine her research methods and plan her data collection.How she attracts moths using UV lights and beer-soaked T-shirtsClinton conducts her fieldwork after sunset, visiting three habitats: deciduous forest, pine forest and meadow. At each location, she uses different methods to attract moths and records the environmental conditions under which they appear.One technique involves ultraviolet lights positioned near a sheet of canvas. The lights attract moths, allowing her to observe and photograph them. She bought one light with money earned from her after-school job shelving books at a local library, while the other was originally intended as a Halloween decoration.She also prepares homemade bait using mushy bananas, brown sugar and beer. She soaks a T-shirt in the mixture and places it over a gardening cage to attract moths that might not gather around the lights.Her father, Brian Clinton, a physician, drives her to and from the nature preserve and buys the beer she needs for the bait. Although he accompanies her on the expeditions, he does not help collect the research data.During each outing, Clinton photographs the moths she encounters and records environmental measurements, including temperature, air pressure and humidity. She also considers weather conditions and moon phases as part of her investigation into variations in moth diversity and abundance.After photographing the insects, she releases them rather than keeping them as specimens. This approach reflects her affection for the creatures and her reluctance to harm them.The importance of her researchMoths are among the most diverse groups of insects, yet they often receive less public attention than butterflies and bees. Clinton's project aims to document which species inhabit the preserve and investigate how moth diversity and abundance vary across different habitats and environmental conditions.Comparing observations from deciduous woodland, pine forest and meadow can help researchers investigate differences in the species recorded in each environment. Recording weather conditions and moon phases also provides information that can help scientists interpret variations between sampling sessions.Her mentor, Dombroskie, believes the dataset could remain useful long after the project concludes. According to The New York Times, her observations may help researchers improve their understanding of moth distribution in the area, particularly among common species that have received relatively little scientific attention.Biodiversity surveys can establish a baseline against which future observations can be compared, helping scientists investigate changes in species distributions and seasonal activity. However, documenting moths alone cannot establish long-term population declines or determine how effectively individual species pollinate plants.Clinton earned recognition among university researchersClinton presented preliminary findings from her research at the Lepidopterists' Society's annual meeting in June 2026, held at the Carnegie Museum of Natural History in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.The society brings together people interested in the study of butterflies and moths, including professional researchers, students and amateur naturalists. Its annual meeting provides opportunities for participants to present their work and exchange scientific knowledge.Clinton entered a student research competition with a poster outlining her preliminary findings from the three habitats. Her competitors included college and graduate students with experience in scientific research.Dombroskie initially doubted that she would win against such an experienced field of participants. Nevertheless, according to The New York Times, Clinton secured second place in the competition.The achievement brought recognition to her independent fieldwork and demonstrated how a high school student could undertake a substantial biodiversity survey with appropriate guidance.Following the completion of her fieldwork, Clinton plans to analyse her observations and submit her findings to academic journals.The overlooked role of moths in pollinationMoths are important nocturnal pollinators, transferring pollen between flowers as they feed on nectar. A 2023 University of Sussex-led study at 10 sites in south-east England found that moths could be effective pollinators despite making fewer visits than daytime insects. Their contribution varies across plant species and environments. Moths also play a vital role in food webs, providing food for birds, bats and other insect-eating animals.As scientists investigate insect declines, studying moth diversity can help reveal changes in ecosystems. A 2021 review published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that moth population trends vary by region and species, with declines documented in several areas. Clinton’s research could help improve understanding of moth diversity while encouraging people to appreciate these often-overlooked insects, many of which have striking colours, intricate patterns and specialised adaptations.How digital tools help her identify mothsPhotographing a moth is only the first step in Clinton's research. She must also identify the species and organise her observations for analysis.She uses iNaturalist, a citizen-science platform that allows people to document wildlife observations and seek help identifying organisms. Other naturalists and specialists can suggest identifications, helping users distinguish between species that may look similar.Clinton also consults field guides covering moths found in the northeastern United States and online resources such as BugGuide.Identification can be challenging because some species have similar wing patterns, while others are so small that their distinguishing characteristics are difficult to see without magnification.By combining photographs, field guides and assistance from other naturalists, Clinton builds a record of her observations without having to collect and preserve every insect she encounters.she wants to become a zoo veterinarianDespite her enthusiasm for moths, Clinton does not plan to become a professional entomologist. One reason is that some forms of insect research involve collecting and killing specimens for examination and preservation.She is uncomfortable with the idea of killing insects for scientific purposes and prefers to photograph and release the moths she encounters.Instead, she plans to study animal science at university and pursue a career as a zoo veterinarian.Her fascination with insects continues beyond her scheduled fieldwork. The newspaper report describes how she once encountered a greater red dart moth in a school hallway, identified it and released it.Clinton planned to end her data collection in October, when the number of adult moths active in the area begins to decline. She then intended to complete her analysis and submit her findings to academic journals.

articles.title: Investigadores de Australia desarrollan cucarachas cibernéticas: son capaces de inyectar medicamentos a las víctimas atrapadas bajo los escombros
articles.standfirst: Los "Paraborgs" se manejan con un mando de videojuegos y llevan cámaras o jeringas a la espalda
articles.summary: Los "Paraborgs" se manejan con un mando de videojuegos y llevan cámaras o jeringas a la espalda
articles.body: Imagina que un terremoto te deja atrapado bajo los escombros y, de repente, ves acercarse una cucaracha gigante con una aguja a la espalda. La escena parece de pesadilla, pero podría convertirse en una de las herramientas de rescate del futuro. Investigadores de la Universidad de Queensland y de la Universidad de Nueva Gales del Sur, en Australia, han convertido cucarachas en pequeños socorristas cibernéticos. Los han bautizado como "Paraborgs", y su objetivo es llegar a víctimas a las que los equipos de rescate no pueden acceder. El trabajo se ha publicado en la revista Advanced Science. Los científicos eligieron la cucaracha excavadora gigante, una especie australiana que pesa unos 40 gramos y puede cargar más de la mitad de su peso. A cada insecto le colocaron una mochila electrónica con electrodos en las antenas y en la parte trasera del cuerpo. Con un mando de videojuegos, los investigadores pueden guiarlas a izquierda o derecha, hacerlas avanzar o detenerlas. Trabajan en equipo: unas llevan una cámara para localizar a la víctima y otras, un inyector con un muelle que dispara una jeringa cargada de medicamento. En las pruebas de laboratorio, las cucarachas recorrieron un circuito de 2,5 metros con éxito en los 25 intentos y acertaron la inyección en el 72 % de los casos. Por ahora, las pruebas se han hecho sobre dianas de silicona y piel de cerdo, no sobre personas. "No estamos sugiriendo que sea un dispositivo médico listo para usarse hoy en personas", advierte T. Thang Vo-Doan, director del laboratorio de biorrobótica de la Universidad de Queensland. Quedan retos por resolver, como la comunicación dentro de edificios derrumbados, la elección de fármacos y dosis o la regulación. El equipo también es consciente del susto que podría provocar ver llegar a uno de estos insectos. Para tranquilizar a las víctimas, plantea incorporarles luces, marcas de emergencia o incluso un pequeño altavoz que diga "la ayuda está en camino".

articles.title: Elon Musk’s dust-up with Ukraine on Starlink isn't over yet
articles.summary: Ukrainian drone advisors have disputed Musk's accusation that Kyiv's forces used Starlink's civilian-only service to conduct drone strikes.
articles.body:
Elon Musk has accused Ukrainian forces of using commercial Starlink in drone strikes.

But two Ukrainian drone figures say the claim is impossible because of limits imposed on the terminals.

It comes after Ukraine was hit by a 10-day slowdown on Starshield, the military version of Starlink.

Ukraine said its access to Starshield was restored this weekend, but Elon Musk isn't finished with Kyiv yet.

In an X post on Sunday, Musk accused Ukrainian forces of breaching Starlink's terms of service by using the civilian platform in drone attacks.

"Ukraine military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," wrote the SpaceX owner .

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," he added.

Musk made it clear he was talking about the commercial platform and not Starshield, the military version of the satellite communications service owned and controlled by the US government.

"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is NOT a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk added.

Two prominent Ukrainian drone figures, however, disputed Musk's statement, saying that it was technically impossible for any of Kyiv's troops to have independently used Starlink in drone strikes.

"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say for sure that this is not true," wrote Serhii Sternenko, a former advisor for drones to Ukraine's defense ministry, on his Telegram channel.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk does not know about the restrictions on Starlink operation in Ukraine," wrote Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, another former advisor.

Both worked in the ministry in early 2026, when it negotiated with SpaceX to prevent Russia from using black-market Starlink terminals in the war. SpaceX agreed in February to block Starlink over Ukraine and Russia, allowing access only to whitelisted Ukrainian terminals.

Sternenko said that Ukrainian civilians and troops could register their terminals on the whitelist , but that these would only work while subject to a speed requirement.

For one to connect while moving, it would have to be put on a special list that uses Starshield instead, he said.

"That is, it was technically impossible to use civilian Starlink to perform missions on drones. All drone missions that required satellite communication could only be carried out using Starshield," Sternenko added.

Beskrestnov said the Ukrainian Starlink terminals were subject to a speed limit of 90 kmph, or about 55 mph. The civilian service is also completely cut off over Russia, he added.

"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and middle strikes," Beskrestnov wrote.

Tactical drones operating on the Ukrainian battlefield at speeds below 55 mph, such as first-person-view attack drones , typically use radio-frequency signals rather than satellite communication to maintain contact with an operator. These are also often too small and lack enough onboard power to reliably carry even a Starlink Mini terminal.

What Ukraine usually uses satellite internet for — hence its reliance on Starshield — is mid-range and deep strikes on Russia's rear or Russian territory, with larger, more powerful drones that fly much faster.

Kyiv also relies on satellite communications for its small interceptor drones, which fly at up to 265 mph to catch incoming attack drones.

Musk followed up on his Sunday X post with a screenshot of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy writing on social media in mid-October that Kyiv's forces "also use Starlink for mid-range strikes" against Russian targets.

However, Zelenskyy's post was describing Ukraine's recent troubles with Starshield, and he repeatedly used the term "Starlink" to refer broadly to the military satellite service instead.

Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider.

Earlier this month, Ukraine raised the alarm that its access to Starshield was being throttled at high speeds, reducing its ability to conduct deeper strikes and to control interceptor drones.

The crisis lasted 10 days and came as President Donald Trump and Musk openly criticized Ukraine for targeting Russian oil facilities at a time when the White House was trying to ease fuel prices.

The Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed US officials and sources, that Musk had personally ordered the speed cap. Musk and Trump have separately said they were not responsible for the slowdown.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Starshield services were running normally again.

articles.title: Moderate drinking harmless? A major new study found that having just two alcoholic drinks a day is linked to a 1 in 25 lifetime risk of dying from alcohol-related causes, challenging a long-held belief
articles.summary: For years, having a drink with dinner or sharing a couple of drinks with friends has often been treated as a relatively harmless habit, provided it does
articles.body: For years, having a drink with dinner or sharing a couple of drinks with friends has often been treated as a relatively harmless habit, provided it does not turn into heavy drinking. But new research suggests that consuming what many people consider a moderate amount of alcohol may carry a greater long-term health risk than they realise.A major analysis published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs estimated that people who consume an average of two alcoholic drinks a day face a 1-in-25 lifetime risk of dying from an alcohol-related cause. The researchers also found no overall protective health effect from alcohol, challenging the belief that light or moderate drinking is necessarily good for health. The findings come from the Alcohol Intake and Health Study, led by researchers from the United States and Canada.What did the researchers find?The researchers examined how different levels of alcohol consumption were associated with the risk of illness, disability and premature death in the US population. They reviewed more than 7,200 scientific publications on alcohol-related diseases and injuries, then combined evidence about those risks with national health and mortality data.Using statistical models, the team estimated the lifetime risk of death attributable to alcohol at different levels of consumption. The analysis found that people drinking an average of 14 standard drinks a week, equivalent to two a day had an estimated 1-in-25 lifetime risk of an alcohol-attributable death.At seven drinks a week, the estimated risk was much lower, at about one in 1,000. The researchers found that risks generally increased as consumption rose, although the size of the risk varied by health condition, age, sex and drinking pattern. The study examined alcohol-related causes of death involving several conditions, including cancers of the mouth, throat and breast, liver disease, cardiovascular conditions and injuries. Kevin Shield, the study's lead author and an associate professor at the University of Toronto, said that the risk continues to increase as alcohol consumption rises.\Does moderate drinking offer any health benefits?One of the study's central findings challenges the idea that drinking small amounts of alcohol provides an overall health advantage. Some earlier research has suggested that light drinking may be associated with a lower risk of certain cardiovascular conditions. However, the researchers found no significant overall protective effect when they considered alcohol's links to a broad range of health outcomes. Possible reductions in the risk of some conditions did not outweigh the risks associated with cancer, liver disease, injuries and other alcohol-related problems.The findings do not mean that every person who drinks will develop an alcohol-related illness. They indicate that, when health risks are considered together, the researchers did not find an overall benefit that would justify treating alcohol as a health-promoting habit.What counts as two drinks a day?The study used the US definition of a standard drink, which contains approximately 13.6 grams of pure alcohol. Depending on alcohol content, this is roughly equivalent to 355 ml of regular beer, 148 ml of wine or 44 ml of spirits. Actual servings can contain more alcohol than these standard amounts. A large glass of wine or a strong beer, for example, may count as more than one standard drink.The researchers found that the risks associated with drinking became more pronounced above approximately seven drinks per week. Their analysis also suggested that people under 40 may face particular risks from alcohol-related injuries and other causes of premature death.What does the study mean for drinking habits?The findings offer a reason to reconsider the assumption that drinking two alcoholic beverages every day is harmless simply because it is not usually classified as heavy drinking. For people who drink, reducing the amount and frequency of consumption can lower exposure to alcohol-related risks. It is also important to remember that the same number of drinks can produce different risks depending on how they are consumed. Several drinks in one sitting may pose additional dangers compared with spreading them across different occasions.The analysis has limitations. Its estimates are based on US health and mortality data. The precise figures may not translate directly to every population or individual.

articles.title: Nasa's 2028 Moon landing plan: SpaceX, Blue Origin race to build lunar landers
articles.summary: Nasa is ramping up preparations for a crucial lunar mission in 2027, with SpaceX and Blue Origin racing to develop landers for the agency’s planned return
articles.body: Nasa is ramping up preparations for a crucial lunar mission in 2027, with SpaceX and Blue Origin racing to develop landers for the agency’s planned return of astronauts to the Moon in 2028.Nasa plans to send astronauts to the moon in 2028. However, in 2027, the agency will undertake a complex space mission in low Earth orbit, called Artemis III, as part of preparations for the crewed lunar landing.According to a Nasa press statement, “Artemis III will carry Nasa astronauts Randy Bresnik, Frank Rubio and Andre Douglas, along with European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano, aboard the Orion spacecraft”.“During the planned 14-day mission, the crew will conduct demonstrations with test versions of lunar landers being developed by Blue Origin and SpaceX,” it said.The test is intended to help Nasa determine which lander is ready for Artemis IV, currently scheduled for early 2028. During the mission, astronauts and flight controllers will practise rendezvous, docking, habitation and operational procedures.The mission aims to reduce risks, validate hardware and build operational experience before a crewed landing attempt.On Friday, Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman reaffirmed the agency’s commitment to launching the low-Earth orbit test mission next year, despite the technical challenges faced by both companies.“We will not delude ourselves into believing that more time, more money, and flying less will somehow make our work safer or more achievable,” Isaacman said at a press conference.The mission is expected to mark the first time astronauts land on the Moon since the Apollo programme ended in 1972.SpaceX, Blue Origin face technical hurdlesSpaceX plans to use its Starship vehicle as a lunar lander, while Blue Origin is developing its Blue Moon Mark 2. Neither vehicle has flown with astronauts aboard or docked with a spacecraft carrying a crew, CNN reported.SpaceX must complete a prototype for Artemis III and demonstrate key systems, including landing legs and an airlock. It also plans to test transferring propellant between two Starship vehicles in Earth orbit, a procedure necessary for the spacecraft’s journey to the Moon.Nasa officials confirmed Elon Musk’s estimate that a lunar landing could require six to eight Starship launches, but said the final number would depend on the results of propellant-transfer tests. CNN reported.Blue Origin, meanwhile, needs to resume New Glenn launches and conduct the delayed test flight of its smaller Blue Moon Mark 1 lander, expected early next year. The Blue Moon Mark 2 vehicle intended for Artemis III must also be equipped with life-support systems and dock with at least three boost stages.Nasa has also made changes to other elements of the programme, including the Space Launch System rocket, Orion spacecraft and lunar spacesuits, to simplify designs and accelerate development.The space agency has yet to decide whether SpaceX or Blue Origin will provide the lander for Artemis IV, saying it intends to use whichever vehicle is ready first amid competition with China, which aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.

articles.title: Meet Siddharth Vikram, the Massachusetts eighth grader who turned his brother's car accident and recovery into an idea for a game-based rehabilitation app, winning a $25,000 national prize
articles.summary: When Siddharth Vikram watched his older brother go through long physical therapy sessions after a serious car accident, he noticed a major problem with
articles.body: When Siddharth Vikram watched his older brother go through long physical therapy sessions after a serious car accident, he noticed a major problem with the recovery process. While clinic visits offered expert help, doing the same exercises at home often left patients feeling bored and unmotivated. Wanting to help, the eighth grader from Carlisle, Massachusetts, used his family's experience to create a new solution. He developed ReHappy, an interactive app that turns repeated physical therapy exercises into fun, game-based challenges for children and teenagers recovering from injuries. His invention earned him national recognition and the $25,000 grand prize in the grades 5 to 8 business category of the Mott Million Dollar Challenge. The nationwide competition, funded by the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation, encourages young people across the United States to share business ideas that solve everyday problems.Turning personal hardship into innovationThe idea for ReHappy came from watching his brother's long recovery and understanding what he was going through. Siddharth saw that while medical professionals provide excellent care, young patients often struggle to keep up with their exercises at home. "He did it with such vigor that I was definitely convinced that those were the most effective ways to do therapy," Siddharth said in an official Q&A published by the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation, describing the care his brother received. "And then when I thought about accessibility, a lot of people can't go to the in-person centers. They're doing it at home on their computers. There's nothing fun." ReHappy aims to solve this problem by turning physical therapy exercises into game levels. Rather than simply checking off completed exercises, the app turns body movements into games. It gives young users quick feedback and encouragement as they work through their recovery plans at home.Perseverance through previous setbacksWinning the national prize did not happen overnight for the young inventor. Siddharth had entered other competitions with early versions of his software. He faced rejection at first, but used those experiences to improve his presentation for the Mott Million Dollar Challenge. "No, I've gone through many pitch competitions for other ideas and for ReHappy itself," Siddharth explained in his interview with the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation when asked if this was his first pitch. "I submitted a video for ReHappy to another competition. It didn't get selected, but it did provide me with valuable insight on how I should craft my video, which really helped me with the Mott Challenge." When the competition judges asked him which key qualities had helped him as an entrepreneur, Siddharth pointed to empathy, grit and growth. His hard work paid off when his family received the official results. "I remember one thing: I was jumping with joy," Siddharth recalled in the foundation feature. "I got the notification and I just ran down and immediately told my dad, and he was also so happy, and we just started instantly formulating a plan for the next steps forward. I was like, 'Wow! These people actually believe in my idea. They're giving me a chance to prove its worth.' It was just really amazing for me."Next steps for the rehabilitation appThe $25,000 prize will help Siddharth continue developing ReHappy. He is also seeking technical advice and support to bring the project closer to being used in clinical care. "ReHappy can definitely go places, and I'm very excited to pursue them," Siddharth told the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation. "I've contacted some people that could really help me work on my idea, give me advice and the help I would need to pursue it. I'm definitely excited for this journey to continue." Siddharth plans to work with healthcare advisers and software developers to improve the app's ability to track body movements. These improvements will help ensure that the platform is safe, accurate and engaging for young patients as they recover from injuries.
