articles.title: Verizon says SpaceX needs up to 8 years and a half trillion dollars to compete in wireless
articles.summary: Verizon's CEO said he's assuming SpaceX will flawlessly execute its US ambitions, but those goals will require massive capital commitments.
articles.body:
Verizon's CEO says he assumes SpaceX will flawlessly execute its US ambitions — but he's not worried.

In order for Starlink to compete, it will still need a lot of land-based infrastructure.

That building could require SpaceX to spend a half trillion dollars over up to eight years, he said.

In business, as in war, the safest bet is often to avoid underestimating your competitors, even when the odds appear to be in your favor.

Verizon CEO Dan Schulman says he's a student of that philosophy when it comes to Elon Musk's ambitions to develop SpaceX's Starlink into a significant US network player.

"Clearly, the tech and the wireless landscape is rapidly evolving, and we need to rapidly evolve along with that," he said during the company's third-quarter earnings call Monday. "I also operate under the assumption that everything SpaceX says they will do, they will do, and that they will execute flawlessly."

Setting aside Musk's track record of delivering on his eyebrow-raising promises , Schulman said there are significant technical and financial hurdles that Starlink would have to clear to meaningfully compete with established networks like Verizon. But it is possible.

"If they build a terrestrial network, it will basically look and feel like every other network," he said. "I think we should take it quite seriously."

News earlier this month that Starlink had acquired a batch of mobile-friendly low-band spectrum sent the share prices of the major US mobile carriers falling by approximately 10% . Verizon is the only one of the three to partially recover from the drop.

"Their service just can't compete with a terrestrial network in suburban and urban areas, where like 98% of our revenues are," he said of the satellite-based system. "We're somewhere between 100 to 1000 times more efficient than they are."

Building a competitive US network, especially for mobile, would require building as many as 80,000 large cell towers on Earth linked with some combination of satellites and fiber optics, Schulman said.

Schulman estimates that project would cost up to a half trillion dollars over six to eight years, with a minimum of four to six years to actually build out the network.

"Then they need to build retail customer service, back office systems, et cetera., and all of that gets them basically the same network and same capabilities and same cost structure as what we have today," Schulman said.

After the call, Musk responded to the forecast with a post on X: "Will take 2 or 3 years."

The Verizon chief's remarks come less than a week after his AT&T counterpart, John Stankey, brushed off concerns that Starlink's mobile network could pose a threat to his business.

"I wouldn't over-rotate on what I would call one carrier of low band spectrum," he said.

articles.title: SpaceX locks in $40B GPU financing deal with Apollo | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.
articles.body:
SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday . In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing” .

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.

SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.

The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.

Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”

The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business . SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.

The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.

While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X . “Some will make it through, but not many.”

articles.title: Everything old is new again with the Fitbit Edge
articles.summary: The $180 Fitbit Edge is a sleek return to the days of simpler fitness tracking bands. All the basics, but not much more.
articles.body: Last week, I sank into my living room couch and watched a bedraggled, nihilistic Matthew McConaughey take a drag of a cigarette in season 1 of True Detective. “You know, someone once told me time is a flat circle. Everything we’ve done, or will do, we’re gonna do over and over and over again.” I assume most people aren’t thinking about fitness trackers or gadgets while watching that scene. But in that moment, I couldn’t help but think about the Fitbit Edge on my wrist. The $179.99 Edge is a modernized version of the 2014-to-2020 era of fitness bands — your Charges, your Altas, your Inspires. If you’ve ever owned one, you already know the vast majority of what the Edge is like. It’s lightweight. You swipe on a small display that shows you basic health and fitness metrics. It lasts for about a week on a charge — though that shrunk down to about a day and a half with the always-on display enabled. It’s a device that isn’t trying to be much more than what it is. [Product: Fitbit Edge | The difference is that the Edge feels more refined on the wrist. Where the Fitbit Charge 6’s display felt boxy, the Edge is fully rounded, giving it a softer vibe. The straps are interchangeable, but with an easier button-release system. The metal link bracelet gives it a more jewelry-like feel, though it costs almost as much as the Edge itself at $150. I’m partial to the $60 magnetic strap, which mimics leather despite being made of silicone. The widgets borrow heavily from the Pixel Watch’s Material 3 Expressive redesign. Though to be clear, this is a proprietary Fitbit OS, not Wear OS. Some of the new watchfaces are elegant, though others highlight the Edge’s big black bezels. (Some things truly never change.) Functionally, it’s also a step above the Fitbit Air. There’s built-in GPS for tracking walks and runs without your phone. You can have alarms, view notifications, and control music. You can’t take calls on the wrist — there are no microphones or speakers. Contactless payments are also a no-go. Andy Abramson, head of product at Google Health, says that’s because “less than one percent [of Charge 6 owners] used the feature” and that Google instead prioritized a “sleek design, altimeter, and weeklong battery.” That walks back some of the advancements that have come to the Charge lineup over the years, but if you want to put a silver lining on that, it narrows the Edge’s focus. This is a fitness tracker. There’s some glanceable information, but there’s absolutely no smartwatch creep here. [Image: [Image: [Image: The big software change is the demise of the Fitbit app as we knew it. It’s Google Health now, with an AI coach if you pony up for the yearly subscription. (You get three months free with purchase; otherwise it’s $10 monthly.) I’ve written about the overall experience in my Fitbit Air review. The broad strokes are the same, though in the months since, Google has spent a lot of time tinkering with and iterating on it. Most notably, the company has beefed up automatic activity tracking. To test this, I tracked a handful of runs on the Edge without officially starting an activity. I then compared that to one tracked by an Apple Watch Ultra 4 and my iPhone’s Runna app. I was surprised, but noticed limitations. For example, on a 2.4-mile run with a five-minute warmup walk and cooldown, the Edge correctly identified the exact moment my warmup transitioned into a legit run and then back into a walk. The estimated distance was also pretty decent at 2.55 miles. It wasn’t quite as good at gauging my running speed. It logged me as running a 10’49” mile pace, whereas my actual pace according to the Apple Watch and my phone was 11’38”. This pattern was fairly typical across my testing, so it’s more that this is a nifty way to still “get credit” if you forget to track an activity. Otherwise, the AI coach is still a Chatty Cathy and requires some weekly hand-holding to get the most out of it. I’ll say it again: The Google Health app can feel cluttered, and I get tripped up looking for information that used to be easy to find, like past workouts. However, if you’re new to fitness and want guidance in creating and sticking to a custom AI-generated routine, this is still the best experience I’ve had so far. The bar is in hell, though, and beware what you initially share with the coach. I regret ever telling it I used to have shin splints, as it remains convinced my perfectly fine shins are in danger of disintegrating with every run. [Image: It’s still such a Chatty Cathy. I wish I could tell you about the Health Guardian features, which should let Fitbit Edge users see noninvasive insulin resistance and blood pressure trends. Alas, the way my testing schedule worked out, I have to wait until November 1st to get my initial results. All in all, I enjoyed the Fitbit Edge as a low-key tracker. This will appeal to folks who just want the basics, but aren’t willing to commit to the screenless life. I’m thinking of the Vergecast listeners who occasionally write in, wondering what happened to simple fitness bands, tired of the smartwatch agenda that took over the past few years. The only gripe I really have is $179.99 feels a tad expensive for what you’re getting. Especially since the Fitbit Air is only $99, and for iPhone users, the Apple Watch SE 3 starts at $249. Brands like Xiaomi and Amazfit also offer much cheaper trackers with displays, even if they’re not quite as sleek on the wrist. You have to admit: It’s kind of funny that in 2026 we’ve gone full circle and come back to this particular form factor. For the past two weeks of testing, I felt like I’d been blasted back to what I thought was a bygone era in my career. My bet is still on smartwatches being the dominant wrist-based wearable in the years to come. However, this renewed yearning for simpler trackers feels significant at a time when AI health and fitness coaches demand more data in increasingly invasive ways. There’s a growing weariness that can’t be ignored — and yet for many of us, it’s not fully practical to truly log off with a screenless device. So if that’s you, the Edge is here because hey — time truly is a flat circle. --- Agree to Continue: Google Fitbit Edge Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Google Fitbit Edge, you must pair it with an iPhone or Android smartphone. That includes the phone’s Terms of Service, privacy policy, and any other permissions you grant. The same goes for any third-party health integrations with other services. For example, if you choose to upload your medical records, you’re agreeing to use CLEAR for identity verification — meaning you’d be agreeing to CLEAR’s terms of service and privacy policies too. There are several optional permissions for things such as location, Bluetooth, camera, background app refresh, notifications, and cellular data. By setting up the Fitbit Edge, you’re agreeing to: * Fitbit Terms of Service * Google Health Additional Terms of Service * Google Health Data and Privacy Policy (formerly Fitbit) If you’re concerned about your health data being used to train Google’s AI, that option is turned off by default and must be opted in to. Similarly, the terms and conditions for Google’s acquisition of Fitbit require that your health data be stored separately and not used for Google’s targeted ad business. Final Tally: three mandatory agreements, several optional permissions

articles.title: For 100 plus years people in distant parts of the world have reported seeing hundreds of tiny, colourful humans after eating certain wild mushrooms, and scientists say they have now identified the mushroom behind it
articles.summary: For nearly a century, people living thousands of miles apart have described a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or
articles.body: For nearly a century, people living thousands of miles apart have described a bizarre experience after eating certain wild mushrooms: seeing dozens or even hundreds of tiny, brightly dressed human figures moving through the real world. Now, researchers have identified a mushroom species linked to these unusual visions in China and the Philippines. According to a report published by ScienceDaily, researchers at the University of Utah used DNA sequencing to identify the fungus as Lanmaoa asiatica. However, the chemical responsible for the hallucinations remains unknown.The findings, published in the journal Mycologia, offer new evidence that the remarkably similar experiences reported in different regions may have a biological explanation. They also reopen a scientific mystery that researchers struggled to solve for decades.A strange phenomenon reported across continentsThe visions are known as Lilliputian hallucinations, a term referring to the perception of miniature people or other tiny figures. The name comes from Lilliput, the fictional land inhabited by tiny people in Jonathan Swift’s novel 'Gulliver’s Travels'.People experiencing these hallucinations have described miniature figures walking across furniture, climbing walls, moving around everyday objects and interacting with their surroundings. Some accounts describe figures resembling elves or clowns wearing colourful clothing. The visions can appear vivid and convincing, rather than like fleeting images.The scientific investigation dates back to 1934, when Western researchers learnt of reports from Papua New Guinea describing miniature-human visions after people ate wild mushrooms. The phenomenon became known as “mushroom madness”.During the 1950s and 1960s, anthropologists and mushroom specialists investigated the reports and considered several species belonging to the Boletaceae family, which includes bolete mushrooms. Chemical investigations, however, failed to establish what might be causing the unusual effects.Samples were even examined by Albert Hofmann, the Swiss chemist known for isolating psilocybin and discovering the effects of LSD. Researchers were unable to identify a substance that explained the visions. Some scientists consequently questioned whether the mushrooms were responsible, and investigations largely faded by the end of the 1960s.Reports from China provide a new clueThe mystery resurfaced in the 1990s, when people in Yunnan province in southwestern China reported similar experiences after eating bolete mushrooms. The mushrooms were known locally as “Jian shou qing”, but identifying the exact species responsible for the hallucinations remained a challenge.The fungus is now known as Lanmaoa asiatica, a mushroom that grows in association with pine trees and is eaten in parts of China. It is prized for its savoury flavour and sold in markets and restaurants during the mushroom season, generally between June and August.In Yunnan, the unusual effects are familiar enough that diners are warned to wait until the mushroom has been cooked thoroughly. Eating it raw or inadequately cooked has been associated with hallucinations and illness.A further clue emerged in 2024, when Colin Domnauer, a doctoral researcher at the University of Utah, learnt of similar experiences among an Indigenous community in the northern Cordillera region of the Philippines. People there described a wild edible mushroom called “Sedesdem” that could cause visions of miniature humans.The reports were striking because they resembled accounts from China and Papua New Guinea, despite the geographical distance between the communities.DNA testing links the Chinese and Philippine mushroomsDomnauer travelled to Yunnan and the Philippines, interviewed local residents and collected mushroom specimens. Researchers then used DNA sequencing to establish the specimens’ identities and examine their evolutionary relationships. The analysis found that the mushrooms known as Jian shou qing in China and Sedesdem in the Philippines belonged to the same species, Lanmaoa asiatica. The discovery also extended the known distribution of the species beyond China.The research team attempted to collect specimens in Papua New Guinea, where the earliest reports originated, but unusually dry conditions prevented them from obtaining suitable samples for genetic comparison.This means the historical Papua New Guinea cases remain unconfirmed at the species level. Although people in all three locations have reported similar visions after eating wild mushrooms, DNA evidence has directly linked the Chinese and Philippine specimens to L. asiatica, not the mushroom described in the earliest accounts.The distinction is important: the research has identified a species associated with the phenomenon in two locations, rather than conclusively proving that every historical report involved the same fungus.The chemical behind the visions remains a mysteryIdentifying the mushroom has not yet revealed how it affects the brain. Researchers found no evidence of familiar psychoactive mushroom compounds, including psilocybin, in their investigation. The results suggest that L. asiatica may contain a previously unidentified substance responsible for the distinctive visions.Scientists have not yet isolated or chemically identified that compound, so its effects on the nervous system remain unclear. The mushroom’s visions also differ from the broader range of experiences commonly associated with psilocybin-containing mushrooms.The researchers hope that identifying the substance could help explain how the brain generates detailed visual experiences. Lilliputian hallucinations are not exclusive to mushroom consumption; they have also been documented in some neurological and medical conditions, including dementia and visual impairment.A consistent biological trigger could therefore offer researchers a way to investigate how these unusual perceptions arise, although any medical application remains speculative.The study also examined the wider diversity of the Lanmaoa genus. Researchers analysed 53 specimens and identified 17 species in the group, including four previously unknown to science. The findings demonstrate how DNA analysis can reveal biological diversity that may have gone unnoticed in specimens already preserved in collections.For now, scientists have made progress on one part of the mystery: identifying the mushroom associated with the tiny-human visions in China and the Philippines. The substance that produces the effect, how it alters perception and whether the same species was responsible for the original Papua New Guinea reports remain open questions.

articles.title: Fusion startups are giving the government shares in exchange for awards. Is it worth it? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Fusion startups face a new challenge, one unrelated to plasma physics: Give the government shares in exchange for funding awards or go it alone?
articles.body:
The U.S. government has long had an on-again, off-again relationship with the fusion power sector. As of last week, it’s definitely back on.

Helion and Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) received awards totaling $260 million from the Department of Commerce under the CHIPS and Science Act, the 2022 law that funds domestic semiconductor development, to develop advanced semiconductors used to help power and control their reactors. Helion landed $175 million , while CFS reeled in $85 million .

But as with many recent government awards, these come with strings attached. Helion and CFS have agreed to give the government non-voting shares in return. With these awards, the fusion industry is finally getting the government’s attention, though maybe not the sort it envisioned.

In the past, government support for a startup meant non-dilutive capital, meaning money that doesn’t shrink existing investors’ ownership percentages, while giving the company a bigger war chest. Investors loved the deals because it meant their startups got more money without them having to pony up. The government doled out the cash to boost American innovation, though it also meant that, in most cases, the government didn’t directly benefit when it picked a winner.

The Trump administration has been pushing to change that calculus.

For both companies, the total dollar amount pales in comparison to how much each has raised . CFS has raised about $4 billion, while Helion is close behind with $3.2 billion in committed capital. The awards are perhaps more important as signals that, after years of cutting and then trickling out fusion funding, the U.S. government is back in the game.

Fusion. which generates power by fusing atoms together as the sun does, is an expensive endeavor, requiring exotic materials, sophisticated computer modeling, and complex manufacturing. Progress over the last decade has attracted private investors who have bet more than $14 billion that one or more companies will be able to put a power plant on the grid.

Yet according to the Fusion Industry Association, the sector’s trade group, that’s still not enough to beat other countries in the race. Last year, the trade group called on the federal government to inject a one-time infusion of $10 billion into the sector, with $5.4 billion intended for fusion startups.

“Other nations are moving aggressively to accelerate their commercial fusion industries, pouring billions in state-backed efforts to win the race to fusion power,” a spokesperson for CFS told TechCrunch. CFS is a member of the Fusion Industry Association. “The $10 billion ask is designed to build out the research infrastructure in the DOE’s Fusion Roadmap and be catalytic for the U.S. domestic fusion industry to compete with China.”

Until recently, the federal government had been dribbling out dollars for fusion. The Biden administration introduced the Milestone Based Fusion Development Program, a Department of Energy program that pays companies as they hit technical goals, but the dollar amounts were paltry; less than $50 million was distributed in the first couple years. More recent awards were a little bigger, but still well shy of money the Fusion Industry Association has called for.

Now, with two companies getting $260 million, it looks like the lobbying may be starting to pay off, though not quite as planned as it comes from Commerce rather than the research budget the Fusion Industry Association sought, and it carries equity strings.

The Fusion Industry Association’s lobbying campaign did not include conversations about equity stakes in exchange for awards, a person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch. Yet Helion said the government will receive $175 million in non-voting equity based on its Series G round, which valued the company at $15.5 billion. That works out to a stake of roughly 1%. The government’s stake in CFS will also be non-voting and based on the company’s most recent valuation, which CFS has not shared publicly. That means the size of the government’s stake in CFS is not known.

“This type of structure has become more common in large U.S. government investments in recent years,” David Kirtley, co-founder and CEO of Helion, told TechCrunch in a statement. “This approach aligns the interests of Helion and the U.S. taxpayer around our commercial success.”

The CFS spokesperson echoed those comments. “This U.S. equity stake will enable the U.S. taxpayer to participate in the upside of our commercial success in exchange for investing in important research and development that supports the growth of an American commercial fusion industry.”

Helion and CFS are the latest in a series of companies that have seen the government take a stake in exchange for federal dollars.

Last year, critical minerals supplier MP Materials gave the government a 15% stake in exchange for a $400 million investment coupled with a $150 million loan, offtake agreements (which are guaranteed purchases of its output), and profit sharing. Another critical minerals company, USA Rare Earth, gave up a 10% stake for a $277 million award and a $1.3 billion loan. And Intel set an even more awkward precedent. The Biden administration had already awarded the company $8.9 billion that hadn’t yet been paid out. Last year, the Trump administration turned that money into a roughly 10% stake in Intel. The list goes on .

Outside the U.S., Germany-based fusion startup Proxima Fusion confirmed to TechCrunch that the German government and the European Union are on its cap table. It also has received equity investments from German government-backed funds including SPRIND (Germany’s federal agency for disruptive innovation) and DCTF (Deutsche Climate Tech Fonds).

Not every fusion startup that has worked with the government has given up equity. Thea Energy and Avalanche Energy, which have received federal awards and contracts, and Pacific Fusion, which has partnered with federal labs, confirmed to TechCrunch that they have not given the government a stake. Inertia Enterprises also told TechCrunch that it had not given the government any equity; the startup has a public-private partnership with the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to commercialize the fusion technology developed there.

So far, it’s just a handful of startups that have agreed to government stakes in exchange for awards. Still, it could set the tone for the industry.

By directly investing in fusion startups, the Trump administration is signaling that fusion power is a strategic priority for the U.S. Such backing could boost investor confidence, though it could just as easily have a chilling effect on private investment. VCs will now have to weigh whether the dilution from a government stake is worth the tradeoff. And what happens to cap tables in case of pay-to-play rounds or wind-downs? Who gets priority?

The fusion industry may have raised billions of dollars in recent years, but it will need billions more to deliver on its promises. Federal awards used to be no brainers when it came time to scale up. Now, they’ve grown more complicated. Will the new bargains be worth it?

articles.title: In 2025, teams began clearing invasive rats and feral pigs from Samoa's Nu'utele Island; by October 2026, sea turtles were nesting after decades of absence, ground-doves were breeding and native seedlings had returned
articles.summary: Sea turtles are nesting on Nu'utele Island in Samoa again after being absent for decades.
articles.body: Sea turtles are nesting on Nu'utele Island in Samoa again after being absent for decades. Their return follows a major conservation effort to remove non-native predators from the uninhabited Pacific island. According to a statement released by global charity Island Conservation on October 20, 2026, conservation teams successfully removed invasive rats and feral pigs from the island. The joint restoration project began in 2025 and involved more than 130 days of fieldwork across 12 separate expeditions, which ended in May 2026. Nu'utele Island is an uninhabited Key Biodiversity Area within a marine protected area off the eastern coast of Upolu. It contains Samoa's best-preserved tropical forest. However, animals brought to the island from elsewhere had damaged local food chains, destroyed native plants and hunted vulnerable wildlife. One year after the removal campaign ended, field surveys show widespread signs of recovery across the island's forests and coastal areas.Native vegetation carpet returning to forestsRemoving invasive mammals has allowed native plants to grow again without being eaten by wild pigs or having their seeds consumed by rats. Forest floors that were once bare are now covered with thick layers of native tree seedlings. In an official statement published by Island Conservation, project manager Paul Jacques described the changes seen during recent monitoring visits. “In many areas, native seedlings are carpeting the forest floor,” Jacques said. “On recent visits, I saw knee-high seedlings growing where forest regeneration had previously been suppressed. People are now able to grow and harvest giant taro plants where crops would have failed previously. These changes point to the recovery of natural processes.” The return of plant life is not limited to the natural forest. Local farming families who visit the island are once again growing important crops, including pineapples, papayas, bananas and giant taro. They can now do so without losing their harvests to destructive wild pigs. As forests grow back, their roots help hold the topsoil in place, reduce coastal erosion and protect natural freshwater supplies during severe weather.Native birds and marine species resume breedingRemoving invasive animals has made the island safer for native and locally unique bird species to nest. Field researchers have been monitoring wildlife and have recorded rapid population growth among several threatened bird species. Nu'utele is home to Samoa's largest remaining population of the rare Shy Ground Dove. This species has been declining across the Southwest Pacific. Within one month of removing the invasive predators, conservation scientists found several active ground-dove nests containing eggs inside bird's-nest ferns. Monitoring teams also found new nests belonging to the Samoan Starling, a species found only in Samoa. They also recorded active breeding behaviour among the Samoan Flycatcher and the Samoan Whistler. With predators gone, sea turtles have also returned to Nu'utele's beaches to lay their eggs after decades of absence. Survey teams also recorded a land crab species that had never before been documented on the island. Land crabs play an important role in moving nutrients between coastal forests, coral reefs and the surrounding ocean. The improved conditions on Nu'utele are also creating opportunities to bring back other species in the future. Island Conservation plans to introduce the Mao, an endangered native Samoan forest bird, to the island as part of its wider 2026 to 2032 Restoring Pacific Islands for Nature and People Project.Regional partnership coordinates complex field operationsRemoving the invasive species required careful planning and cooperation between local communities and international environmental groups. Samoa's Ministry of Natural Resources and Environment led the project alongside traditional landowners and community volunteers from the Aleipata district. Island Conservation provided technical guidance, while the Pacific Regional Invasive Species Management Support Service coordinated regional logistics. The service is managed by the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme. The project received funding from New Zealand's Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade and the United Kingdom International Development through the Predator Free Pacific programme. Bell Laboratories also provided additional operational support.In comments published by Island Conservation, David Moverley, an invasive species adviser at the Secretariat of the Pacific Regional Environment Programme, explained how the project's success could help other Pacific islands prepare for climate challenges. “Nu'utele shows what's possible when communities, governments, and conservation partners work together towards a shared vision,” Moverley said. “We're seeing forests regenerate, native wildlife return, food systems improve, and vital habitat expand for species that depend on healthy ecosystems. The lessons learned from this island can help guide restoration efforts across the Pacific and beyond.” Conservation teams will continue to monitor Nu'utele's ecosystems over the long term. They will track forest growth, study marine life within the nearby protected area and collect information to guide future island restoration projects across the Pacific.

articles.title: Anfíbio de 237 milhões de anos pode ter sido o primeiro a viver no mar | G1
articles.standfirst: Fósseis encontrados na China indicam que animal tinha corpo blindado, brânquias e adaptações para sobreviver na água salgada, algo que nenhum anfíbio atual consegue fazer.
articles.summary: Fósseis encontrados na China indicam que espécie tinha corpo blindado, brânquias e adaptações para sobreviver na água salgada.
articles.body:
Reconstrução artística mostra o anfíbio marinho Gerrothorax maritimus capturando um celacanto por sucção no fundo do oceano. — Foto: Chen Geng/Guizhou University

Um anfíbio que viveu há cerca de 237 milhões de anos pode ter sido o mais antigo de que se tem registro a passar toda a vida no mar, sem precisar retornar à terra firme ou à água doce.

Batizada de Gerrothorax maritimus , a espécie foi descrita a partir de dois esqueletos quase completos encontrados na província de Guizhou, no sul da China.

O estudo foi publicado nesta última segunda-feira (26) na revista científica "Nature Ecology & Evolution".

A descoberta chama atenção porque nenhuma das mais de 8 mil espécies de anfíbios que vivem atualmente é totalmente marinha.

Sapos, rãs e salamandras têm a pele muito permeável , uma característica vantajosa em ambientes úmidos, mas que dificulta a sobrevivência em água salgada.

“Os anfíbios atuais são muito bem adaptados aos ambientes úmidos graças à pele permeável, que permite que respirem e absorvam água sem usar a boca. Mas essa mesma característica trabalha contra o animal no mar”, explicou ao g1 Ryosuke Motani, professor da Universidade da Califórnia em Davis (EUA) e um dos autores do estudo.

Na água do mar, segundo ele, essa pele favorece a perda de água do corpo. Mesmo espécies atuais capazes de tolerar ambientes próximos ao litoral precisam voltar à água doce para se recuperar.

O G. maritimus, contudo, parece ter encontrado outra solução.

O animal tinha o corpo achatado e coberto por uma pesada armadura óssea , que pode ter funcionado como uma barreira contra a perda de água.

Também possuía brânquias e um sistema digestivo que, segundo os pesquisadores, poderiam ter ajudado a eliminar o excesso de sal e absorver a água do mar .

“Essa armadura impediria fisicamente que a água do corpo fosse retirada pela água do mar. O intestino permitiria absorver água, como ocorre nos peixes marinhos, enquanto as brânquias ajudariam a eliminar o sal”, afirmou Motani.

Como os cientistas sabem que ele vivia no mar?

Para os pesquisadores, um dos principais desafios foi determinar se o animal realmente vivia no oceano ou se seus restos foram levados até o ambiente marinho após a morte.

A evidência considerada mais forte disso veio da composição química dos ossos , que revelou uma assinatura semelhante à da água do mar de cerca de 237 milhões de anos atrás.

Outros indícios reforçam essa interpretação. Os esqueletos foram encontrados em rochas formadas a pelo menos 30 quilômetros das ilhas mais próximas , segundo a reconstrução da geografia da região naquele período.

Além disso, pequenos ossos dos dedos permaneceram ligados ao esqueleto. Essas estruturas costumam se soltar rapidamente quando uma carcaça fica à deriva, o que sugere que os animais morreram e foram enterrados perto de onde viviam.

Os fósseis também aparecem associados a grandes ictiossauros , répteis completamente adaptados à vida oceânica.

O Gerrothorax maritimus tinha corpo bastante achatado e provavelmente passava boa parte do tempo no fundo do oceano.

Sua boca era larga e ligada a uma estrutura robusta na região da garganta. Para os pesquisadores, isso indica que o animal provavelmente capturava suas presas por sucção, abrindo a boca rapidamente para puxá-las junto com a água.

“Era um predador por sucção. Sua boca grande e a estrutura forte das brânquias permitiriam sugar a presa”, explicou ao g1 Da-yong Jiang, professor da Universidade de Pequim e também autor do trabalho.

A estratégia seria semelhante à usada atualmente por alguns tubarões que vivem no fundo do mar.

Mesmo assim, ainda há perguntas sem resposta no estudo. Como tecidos moles não foram preservados, os pesquisadores não sabem exatamente como funcionava a fisiologia do animal nem como ele se reproduzia.

Motani diz que há a suspeita de que a espécie pudesse dar à luz filhotes em vez de colocar ovos , o que facilitaria uma vida totalmente marinha. Mas, por enquanto, não há evidência direta que confirme essa hipótese.

Fóssil do anfíbio marinho Gerrothorax maritimus, preservado com a barriga voltada para cima. — Foto: Ryosuke Motani

articles.title: In 2018, scientists pumped 75 kg of red dye into the Atlantic off Martha’s Vineyard; over 36 hours, they found mixing inside the surface layer was about 140 times stronger than across its base

articles.body: In a striking ocean experiment, scientists released 75 kilograms of rhodamine dye into the Atlantic Ocean south of Martha’s Vineyard, Massachusetts, to watch how water moves and mixes beneath the surface. The experiment, conducted on August 16–17, 2018, showed that the dye spread readily within the ocean’s upper mixed layer but crossed into the denser water below far more slowly, according to a study published in Continental Shelf Research on ScienceDirect. The findings offer a detailed glimpse into a part of the ocean that is constantly being stirred by winds, waves and currents, and show just how strongly the ocean’s structure can limit movement between its layers.Why release dye into the ocean?The experiment was not intended simply to watch a colourful plume drift through the sea. The researchers were using rhodamine, a neutrally buoyant chemical tracer, as a marker for a parcel of seawater.The release took place about 28 kilometres south of Martha’s Vineyard. Scientists pumped roughly 130 gallons of a rhodamine-ethanol mixture into the water from the research vessel R/V Connecticut, with the mixture designed to have approximately the same density as the surrounding near-surface seawater.By tracking the dye’s concentration through the water column and combining those measurements with observations of currents, temperature and other water properties, researchers could follow how the water itself was being transported.The ocean has a well-stirred upper layerNear the surface, the ocean contains a region known as the mixed layer. Turbulence generated by processes such as wind and surface forcing continually stirs this layer, helping make its properties relatively uniform with depth. NOAA describes the surface mixed layer as an important zone for exchanges of heat, freshwater, momentum and dissolved gases between the atmosphere and ocean. That vigorous mixing was clearly reflected in the dye experiment.The researchers estimated vertical diffusivity, a measure of how efficiently material spreads vertically, within the mixed layer at approximately 7 × 10⁻⁴ square metres per second.But at the bottom of that layer, where the water becomes more strongly stratified in the region known as the pycnocline, the estimated diffusivity fell to approximately 5 × 10⁻⁶ square metres per second. That means vertical mixing within the mixed layer was about 140 times greater than mixing across its base.Most of the dye stayed near the surfaceOver the roughly 33-hour survey, scientists detected 99% of the dye within the mixed layer. That does not mean the dye never moved downward. Some dye was detected below the mixed layer, but its distribution was patchy and did not closely match the concentrations above it.The researchers suggested that some of the dye found below may have left the mixed layer earlier and at a different location before being carried horizontally by currents. In other words, the ocean’s currents could transport water that had already crossed the boundary, making the dye appear beneath the mixed layer far from where that downward movement originally occurred.A barrier beneath the surfaceThe sharp difference in mixing rates highlights the importance of ocean stratification. Inside the mixed layer, turbulence can distribute a tracer relatively quickly. But beneath it, differences in density make it considerably harder for water and dissolved substances to cross into the stratified ocean below.The researchers concluded that downward penetration from the mixed layer was a slow process occurring over timescales of at least several days, rather than something that happens uniformly within hours. The downward movement also appeared to occur in intermittent, patchy events rather than as a smooth, continuous process.Why the experiment mattersUnderstanding how quickly substances move through the ocean is important far beyond one dye plume. Oceanographers use mixing estimates to improve models of how heat, nutrients, pollutants and other dissolved substances are transported. The researchers also found that the dye’s horizontal movement could largely be explained by currents measured using high-frequency radar, with a relatively small additional contribution from turbulent diffusion.What looked like a simple red plume was therefore a window into a much bigger question: how does the ocean move material around? The experiment showed that the answer depends not only on where the water is flowing, but also on which layer it is in, because beneath the restless surface, the ocean can behave like a surprisingly effective barrier.

articles.title: After 160 years of excavations, archaeologists find a 2,800-year-old bone flute at ancient Troy, offering the first direct evidence of music at the legendary city
articles.summary: For the first time in 160 years of excavations, archaeologists unearthed a musical instrument at Troy, a flute made of bone that dates back about 2,800
articles.body: For the first time in 160 years of excavations, archaeologists unearthed a musical instrument at Troy, a flute made of bone that dates back about 2,800 years. Also discovered was a 4,500-year-old humanoid idol, which archaeologists hope will help shed light on the cultural traditions of the region.The bone flute was found in what's known as the site's Archaic layer, suggesting that the instrument dates back to about the eighth century B.C.E. This pivotal period in classical antiquity is roughly when the first Olympic Games took place and when legend says Romulus and Remus founded Rome. Also at this point in time, Troy was beginning to rise back into importance following centuries of decline.According to the announcement of the discovery made by the Turkish Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the bone flute's head has been preserved while its body has been lost to history. Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy announced the discoveries from the 2026 excavation season, saying the flute provided direct archaeological evidence of musical culture at Troy.Dr Rustem Aslan, the director of the Troy excavations, emphasised the importance of the discovery. “We know about musical instruments from many depictions elsewhere. However, this is the first time a bone flute has been encountered in the history of Troy excavations,” Aslan said.Dating to approximately 750-480 B.C., the instrument provides evidence of music in a period when it played an important role in religious rituals as well as social and public life.Along with the bone flute, researchers found the head of a humanoid idol. The object was unearthed in a fire-damaged archaeological layer dating back to Troy II or the city's Early Bronze Age phase of occupation. During this period, Troy was a fortified settlement, well-connected to other civilisations across western Anatolia due to its position near the Dardanelles Strait.A shocking entry in Troy's archaeological record, the bone flute will hopefully serve as a window into the folkways and culture of everyday people living in Troy 2,800 years ago. Archaeologists noted that the age of the musical instrument is particularly relevant, as it dates back to the same period associated with the legendary Greek poet Homer.The composition of Homer’s epics, the Iliad and the Odyssey, is generally dated to the eighth century B.C.E. — just like the bone flute. However, the precise dating of Homer’s works remains under debate.The Iliad tells the tale of the legendary Trojan War, including the use of the famed Trojan Horse, which occurred (if it actually happened) in Troy. Meanwhile, the Odyssey narrates the story of how the Greek hero Odysseus journeyed home after the war. In Book 10 of the Iliad, Homer describes the Greek king Agamemnon standing over the Trojan plain, marvelling “at the many fires that burned before the face of Ilios, and at the sound of flutes and pipes, and the din of men.” Aslan himself drew the parallel, saying, according to AA, that Homer specialists accept that the poet lived in the eighth century, and that many researchers accept the epics were written down then. Finding such an object in an Archaic layer of the same century was, in his words, quite important for the excavation.If it in fact occurred at all, the Trojan War is usually thought to have taken place around 1200 B.C.E. When Homer was writing about it some four centuries later, he may have included flute-playing in the narrative because it was popular in his time, even if it may not have been popular 400 years earlier.While the coincidence of a flute being found at Troy and a flute at Troy being described by Homer is intriguing, archaeologists stressed that there is no concrete evidence that directly links the instrument to either Homer or his poems.Aslan also highlighted a different coincidence involving the recent film adaptation of the Odyssey. According to Aslan, in order to produce the song of the Sirens for the film, the producers made experimental music with a reconstruction of an eighth-century B.C.E. flute, not unlike the one that was just recently found.

articles.title: La 'Gran Muralla Verde' que nació hace 19 años: ¡hoy cuenta ya con 8.000 kilómetros y cruza diez países en África!
articles.standfirst: Objetivo: detener el avance de la desertificación en la región del Sahel como desafío ecológicos y humanitario
articles.summary: Objetivo: detener el avance de la desertificación en la región del Sahel como desafío ecológicos y humanitario
articles.body: El avance de la desertificación en la región del Sahel es uno de los desafíos ecológicos y humanitarios más críticos del siglo XXI. Para hacerle frente, nació la Gran Muralla Verde del Sáhara y el Sahel, una iniciativa monumental que busca transformar el paisaje africano y asegurar el futuro de millones de personas. Hace 19 años empezó un gran proyecto que hoy se asienta entre la naturaleza. Recibió dicho nombre: Gran Muralla Verde. Una iniciativa impulsada por varios países africanos con el objetivo de restaurar millones de hectáreas degradadas y frenar el avance del desierto del Sáhara. El proyecto nació en 2007, bajo el impulso de la Unión Africana, con una ambición determinada: restaurar 100 millones de hectáreas de tierras degradadas antes de 2030 en la franja del Sahel. Pretendía crear una enorme franja de vegetación que atravesara el continente de oeste a este, desde Senegal hasta Yibuti. Más que una simple barrera de árboles, la iniciativa busca recuperar ecosistemas, mejorar la fertilidad de los suelos y ofrecer oportunidades económicas a millones de personas que viven en algunas de las regiones más vulnerables del planeta. Expertos en la materia, y que han tratado este asunto directamente, afirman que no se trata sólo de plantar árboles, sino de devolver la fertilidad a los suelos, recuperar ecosistemas y ayudar a las comunidades locales a adaptarse a unas condiciones climáticas cada vez más complejas. Abarca más de 8.000 kilómetros y cruza una decena de países africanos entre los que están Burkina Faso, Níger, Nigeria, Etiopía, Eritrea, Malí, Mauritania, Sudán y Chad. Gracias a la reforestación y a técnicas agrícolas sostenibles, ya se han recuperado millones de hectáreas de terreno degradado y se han generado miles de empleos relacionados con la agricultura y la gestión forestal. La falta de financiación, los conflictos armados en algunas zonas y los efectos cada vez más intensos del cambio climático siguen siendo grandes retos. Sin embargo, la Gran Muralla Verde se ha convertido en uno de los mayores proyectos de restauración ambiental del mundo y en un símbolo de la lucha africana contra la desertificación. Etiopía es uno de los líderes indiscutibles del proyecto, habiendo restaurado millones de hectáreas mediante la reforestación de tierras altas y la creación de terrazas agrícolas para evitar la erosión del suelo. El avance se enfrenta a importantes obstáculos. La inestabilidad geopolítica y los conflictos armados en países como Malí, Burkina Faso y la región del lago Chad dificultan el acceso de los técnicos al terreno. Además, el financiamiento internacional prometido a menudo llega de forma lenta o fragmentada, lo que ralentiza las obras de infraestructura hidráulica necesarias.

articles.title: In 2024, a Florida city began a $32 million project at its 209-acre Tucker Ranch preserve; two years later, it opened a 25.6-acre botanical and wellness park after finishing the work for $31 million
articles.summary: A former cattle ranch in Florida has gained a new purpose, bringing botanical gardens, outdoor fitness areas and wellness facilities together in a
articles.body: A former cattle ranch in Florida has gained a new purpose, bringing botanical gardens, outdoor fitness areas and wellness facilities together in a sprawling natural preserve. What began as a multimillion-dollar development project in 2024 has now opened to the public, offering residents a place to explore nature, learn about gardening and take part in health-focused activities.The city of Winter Garden officially opened the 25.6-acre Tucker Ranch Holistic Health and Wellness Park and Botanical Garden on October 23, 2026. According to the City of Winter Garden’s official announcement, the project was completed for $31 million, below the planned budget of approximately $32 million. The new facilities form part of the larger 209-acre Tucker Ranch Park and Nature Preserve, expanding its recreational and educational offerings.A two-year project transforms part of the preserveConstruction began with a groundbreaking ceremony on August 23, 2024. The 25.6-acre development was planned as an expansion of the existing nature preserve, whose first phase opened in 2018. The second phase was designed to offer more than a conventional public park. By bringing together nature, wellness facilities and educational spaces, Winter Garden aimed to create a setting where visitors could exercise, learn about nutrition and gardening, and spend time outdoors.The larger Tucker Ranch property is located at 100 Avalon Road. Its existing amenities include nature trails, a playground, picnic areas and a launch point for canoes and kayaks. Walking paths connect these facilities with the newly opened garden and wellness park.Botanical gardens and trails form the centrepieceThe new park features a botanical garden containing ornamental plants, food-producing plants and varieties intended to attract pollinators. These collections provide a setting for visitors to explore the landscape while learning about plants and their role in the environment. The grounds also include nature paths, a boardwalk and a trail system with exercise stations. A covered pavilion extending over the water, along with a pond and fountain, adds spaces for visitors to pause and enjoy the surroundings.One distinctive feature is the historic West Orange Country Club entrance arch. The city preserved the structure and relocated it within the park to create a prominent entrance to the botanical garden. Together, the landscaped gardens and outdoor amenities are intended to make the site suitable for different types of visits, from daily walks and informal exercise to nature appreciation and family outings.Retreat centre and teaching kitchen expand activitiesBeyond its outdoor facilities, the development includes a 5,000-square-foot Retreat Center with an indoor venue and screened patio. The space is intended to accommodate classes, community programmes and other organised activities. Another facility, The Ranch House, includes a demonstration kitchen, outdoor patio and fireplace. The kitchen can support educational activities centred on cooking, nutrition and food preparation.Edible Learning Gardens provide opportunities for visitors to explore gardening techniques and understand how food can be grown at home or in community settings. These facilities complement the botanical garden by connecting environmental education with everyday health and lifestyle practices. The city has also worked with local health and wellness organisations, including AdventHealth, Orlando Health and Healthy West Orange, to support the broader vision for the property. The aim is to make wellness accessible through a combination of movement, learning, social engagement and time in nature.Historic property gains a new community roleTucker Ranch has a history that predates its development as a public preserve. The property was once associated with the West Orange Country Club, which operated in the early 20th century. During the Second World War, the area also served as Camp Kent, where radar-related testing took place. The Tucker family later operated a cattle ranch on the land, and Tucker's Ranch Campground opened in 1969. The city later gained ownership of the property, paving the way for its development as a public preserve.The new botanical and wellness park builds on that history while giving the land a broader public purpose. Rather than replacing the natural setting with a conventional recreation complex, the project combines constructed amenities with gardens, water features and existing trails.Free public access to the expanded parkThe grand opening took place on October 23, 2026, with a ribbon-cutting ceremony and an opportunity for visitors to tour the new facilities. Admission is free, and the park is open daily. According to the city's published schedule, Tucker Ranch operates from 8 am to 6 pm between March and October, and from 8 am to 5 pm between November and February. Parking and restrooms are available on site.With the second phase complete, Winter Garden has expanded a 209-acre preserve with facilities intended to serve families, nature enthusiasts and people interested in outdoor wellness. The $31 million project brings botanical exploration, exercise, gardening education and community programming together in one public setting.

articles.title: When restaurants closed in 2020, US oyster farmers were left with millions of unsold shellfish; six years later, a rescue programme has bought over 7 million oysters for 35 reef sites and helped protect more than 1,000 aquaculture and related jobs
articles.summary: When restaurants across the United States shut down during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, oyster farmers suddenly lost their biggest market, leaving
articles.body: When restaurants across the United States shut down during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, oyster farmers suddenly lost their biggest market, leaving millions of shellfish unsold and threatening coastal livelihoods. What began as an emergency effort to help struggling growers has since developed into a conservation programme that uses farmed oysters to rebuild damaged marine habitats.According to an October 26, 2026, report by The Pew Charitable Trusts, the Supporting Oyster Aquaculture and Restoration (SOAR) programme has purchased more than 7 million oysters from over 150 growers since 2020. The initiative has supplied oysters and shells to 35 restoration sites across eight states, helped regenerate more than 60 acres of native oyster reefs and helped protect more than 1,000 aquaculture and related jobs. Its approach is now documented in a new handbook intended to help other communities replicate the model.How the pandemic crisis created an opportunity for restorationOyster farming depends heavily on restaurants, which account for a substantial share of the market for these shellfish. When dining establishments closed during the pandemic, farmers found themselves with large quantities of oysters they could not sell through their usual channels. The unsold stock represented not only lost income but also years of investment and labour. At the same time, wild oyster populations along US coastlines had declined significantly because of overharvesting, habitat destruction, pollution and disease. In many areas, the decline was so severe that natural reproduction alone could no longer replenish these populations.The crisis presented an opportunity to address both problems through one intervention. Developed jointly by The Pew Charitable Trusts and The Nature Conservancy, SOAR began purchasing surplus farmed oysters and redirecting them to suitable restoration sites. The programme also received financial support from Builders Vision and the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. Instead of allowing unsold oysters to become a financial loss for growers, the initiative created an additional market while supplying material for rebuilding native reefs.From emergency purchases to 35 restoration sitesSOAR's initial work focused on connecting oyster farmers with restoration projects that could use their shellfish. The programme began in New Hampshire's Great Bay, working with local shellfish farms and the University of New Hampshire to support reef recovery.The approach subsequently expanded to other coastal locations, including New Jersey's Barnegat and Delaware bays. Partners coordinated purchases, transport and deliveries to restoration sites, while working with state agencies, researchers and industry representatives to determine where the oysters could be deployed effectively. The programme established standards for participating growers, oyster quality, inspections and deployment schedules. These measures helped ensure that purchased oysters were suitable for restoration and that deliveries aligned with farming practices and ecological requirements.According to Pew, the initiative has now engaged more than 150 growers and supplied oysters to 35 restoration sites in eight states. The purchases included approximately 1.4 million farmer-grown spat on shell, clusters of young oysters attached to shells that can help establish new reef populations. One project involved collaboration with the Squaxin Island Tribe and the Puget Sound Restoration Fund in Washington state to replant about 71,000 adult native Olympia oysters in Palela Bay. Other efforts have supported reef restoration in Maryland and New York.Why rebuilding oyster reefs mattersThe programme's impact extends beyond helping farmers recover financially. Oyster reefs perform several ecological functions that support coastal environments and communities. Adult oysters filter water as they feed, removing pollutants. When oysters form dense reefs, these structures provide food and shelter for fish, crustaceans and other marine organisms. Healthy reefs can also help reduce shoreline erosion by absorbing wave energy and buffering coastal areas against storms.These benefits are particularly important as coastal communities contend with erosion and increasingly severe weather. Restoring native oyster populations can contribute to healthier marine habitats while supporting the livelihoods of people who depend on coastal industries.SOAR's experience also demonstrates how aquaculture, often associated primarily with food production, can contribute to conservation. Farmed oysters can supplement restoration efforts by providing shellfish that are ready to be transferred to suitable sites, although successful reef recovery also depends on local environmental conditions and appropriate restoration planning.A handbook aims to help other communities replicate the modelAfter six years of work, SOAR's partners have compiled their experience into a handbook titled Partnering With Oyster Growers to Rebuild Reefs. The guide outlines how communities can establish similar partnerships between shellfish farmers, conservation organisations, funders and natural resource managers. It includes case studies, a development checklist and practical advice on selecting restoration sites, establishing partnerships, coordinating purchases and measuring environmental and economic outcomes.The broader SOAR initiative has also expanded beyond its original oyster purchase programme. Its Shellfish Growers Resiliency Fund, launched in 2021, has supported 83 farmer-led projects. Workforce development efforts in 2025 and 2026 have also helped create opportunities for people entering the shellfish industry through internships, training and professional development. Across its various initiatives, SOAR has reached 21 states and Puerto Rico, extending its work beyond the eight states involved in the oyster purchase programme.What began as a response to an unprecedented market disruption has therefore developed into a model linking economic support with marine conservation. By turning surplus oysters into a resource for reef restoration, SOAR has offered coastal communities a practical way to support growers while helping rebuild habitats that protect shorelines and sustain marine life.

articles.title: Elon Musk has a 'failure warning' for these technology companies; says: Investors have already started betting against them
articles.summary: Elon Musk has warned that most “neoclouds”, startups that rent out computing power for artificial intelligence (AI), may not survive as access to funding
articles.body: Elon Musk has warned that most “neoclouds”, startups that rent out computing power for artificial intelligence (AI), may not survive as access to funding becomes harder. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Musk said more than 200 such companies could face closures and consolidation, although a few may survive. He also said lenders have largely stopped providing money to companies that do not earn significant revenue outside AI data centres. In the post, Musk pointed to SpaceX’s ability to raise $40 billion in debt for graphics processing units (GPUs), saying its investment-grade status and revenue from Starlink and rocket launches helped it secure the funding.Elon Musk’s comments come in a reply to a post by Canadian-American venture capitalist Chamath Palihapitiya forecasting excess stranded compute in 2027 from disorganized, undercapitalized neoclouds and slow, bureaucratic hyperscalers prioritizing internal needs over third-party model companies.What are neocloudsNeoclouds are companies that provide cloud computing services mainly for artificial intelligence (AI) and other demanding computing tasks. They offer access to powerful chips, especially GPUs (graphics processing units), which are used to train and run AI models. Traditional cloud providers offer a wide range of services, from data storage and website hosting to databases and software tools. Neoclouds focus more narrowly on providing the computing power needed for AI workloads.Here’s what Chamath Palihapitiya said:“As someone with a portfolio of energized land assets here is what I am seeing:1. Neoclouds are disorganized and poorly capitalized. Some are definitely better than others however.2. Hyperscalers are intractable, bureaucratic organizations that take 3 months to do an NDA and want 18mo escrow periods. We built our portfolio by competing against these terms because of our speed and simplicity. The more future assets orgs like ours win, the bigger the problem for the hyperscalers downstream (see 3).3. There are delays in the existing pipeline that will catch people off guard in 2027. Hyperacalers will (obviously) react by focusing on their own internal compute needs over any third party. If the third party is a model company, they will tell them to go through their model router where they will also take a non-trivial vig. Them telling Ant they have no compute for them (rumored in Ant’s S-1) if true is a huge tell that this is already happening.All of this is to say that it does look like there will be a lot of partially stranded compute and compute sitting in inventory in 2027 than is currently forecasted. This is bought and paid for but effectively underearning (below total cost of capital) or collecting dust. We see this as true for everyone - model companies, hyperscalers, neoclouds except ONE (you can guess which one).This dislocation will benefit two kinds of orgs: the non-bureaucratic big scalers who can build industrial scale quickly and the nimble, well capitalized players feeding them.2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Scientists released marsh rabbits into Florida’s Everglades to test the impact of Burmese python attacks; snakes caused 77% of recorded deaths
articles.summary: For years, scientists suspected that invasive Burmese pythons were contributing to the disappearance of mammals from Everglades National Park in Florida.
articles.body: For years, scientists suspected that invasive Burmese pythons were contributing to the disappearance of mammals from Everglades National Park in Florida. Earlier surveys documented sharp declines as the snakes spread, but they could not establish cause and effect. To investigate the link, researchers from the University of Florida, the U.S. Geological Survey and the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission moved marsh rabbits into the park, fitted them with radio collars and tracked their fate. Among 26 rabbits that survived the first 10 days after release in the park, 17 of 22 recorded deaths were attributed to pythons, accounting for 77% of the total. Three other deaths were attributed to unidentified warm-blooded predators. At control sites outside the park, no rabbits were killed by Burmese pythons. Published in 2015, the experiment provided direct evidence that python predation could prevent marsh rabbit populations from persisting in parts of the Everglades.Why scientists tested Burmese pythons in the EvergladesBurmese pythons (Python bivittatus) are native to Southeast Asia but have established populations in southern Florida, including Everglades National Park. The large constrictors prey on vertebrates. A previous analysis of python stomach contents in the park found that mammals accounted for approximately 75% of their diet, a figure cited by the researchers in their 2015 paper. Scientists had suspected that the snakes were contributing to the disappearance of native mammals for years. A 2012 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences titled Severe mammal declines coincide with proliferation of invasive Burmese pythons in Everglades National Park compared historical observations with later nocturnal road surveys. Before 2000, mammals were frequently encountered during surveys in the park. From 2003 to 2011, surveys covering 56,971 kilometres recorded a 99.3% decline in raccoon observations, a 98.9% decline in opossum observations and an 87.5% decline in bobcat observations. Researchers also failed to detect rabbits. These figures measured the frequency of observations, rather than directly estimating population sizes.The declines coincided geographically and over time with the spread of Burmese pythons. However, the 2012 findings were largely correlational, leaving questions about whether the snakes were responsible for the changes. The 2015 research team chose marsh rabbits because they reproduce throughout the year and can produce up to 6 litters annually, with 3 to 5 young per litter. Their populations can persist under considerable predation pressure, making them useful for testing whether an introduced predator could suppress a native mammal population. Before moving the rabbits, researchers surveyed the park’s study areas but found no evidence of existing rabbit populations at the release sites. They then designed an experiment to compare rabbit survival in areas where pythons were established with survival in areas where the snakes were rare or absent.Radio-collared marsh rabbits reveal python predationThe researchers captured adult marsh rabbits in areas where the animals remained common and tracked them using radio collars equipped with mortality sensors. Between September 2012 and August 2013, the team captured, released and monitored rabbits across several study sites. The researchers released 31 rabbits at 2 locations in Everglades National Park: a coastal marsh and a freshwater wetland. Another 15 rabbits were moved to a procedural control site, while 49 were captured, collared and released at Fakahatchee Strand Preserve State Park, where pythons were rare or absent. These comparison sites helped researchers assess whether mortality differed between areas with established python populations and areas with little or no python activity.The results showed a marked difference. Of the 26 rabbits in the park that survived the first 10 days after release, 22 died during the study. Pythons were identified as the cause of 17 deaths, or 77% of the 22 recorded deaths. Three other deaths were attributed to unidentified endothermic predators, meaning warm-blooded animals. One death was attributed to a known mammalian predator, while another was assigned to a different cause. At the control sites, no rabbits were killed by Burmese pythons. At the main control site, mammalian predators accounted for 71% of deaths with an attributable cause. This percentage excludes deaths whose cause could not be established, unlike the 77% figure for the park, which uses all 22 recorded deaths in its denominator.The researchers also investigated whether the introduced rabbits reproduced in the park. Pellet surveys in February 2013 detected both juvenile and adult rabbit pellets, indicating that reproduction had occurred. Rabbit pellets continued to be detected at the release sites until June 2013. The last radio-tracked rabbit in the park died in July 2013. In December 2013, about 15 months after the initial release, researchers searched the original 5 hectares of habitat and an additional 10 hectares used by tracked rabbits. They found no rabbit pellets at either release site. The findings indicated that, despite evidence of breeding earlier in the experiment, the introduced rabbit populations had not persisted.A later study examined where marsh rabbits remainedA separate study published in Biological Invasions in 2016 titled Invasive pythons, not anthropogenic stressors, explain the distribution of a keystone speciesexamined the distribution of marsh rabbits across the Greater Everglades ecosystem. Led by Adia Sovie and colleagues, the research assessed whether python invasion or other environmental pressures could explain where rabbits continued to occur.The team examined distance from the centre of the python invasion alongside factors including altered hydrology, habitat characteristics, mercury contamination and human development. The researchers found that distance from the invasion’s epicentre best explained marsh rabbit occurrence in suitable habitat patches. None of the alternative stressors examined could explain the observed distribution. The estimated probability of finding marsh rabbits in suitable habitat ranged from zero at the invasion’s epicentre to nearly 1 at locations about 150 kilometres away. The findings supported the hypothesis that invasive pythons were shaping the distribution of marsh rabbits in southern Florida. The 2016 study complemented the earlier experiment. The 2015 research tracked the fate of introduced rabbits and documented high mortality from python predation, while the later study examined the broader geographic pattern of rabbit occurrence.What the findings mean for Everglades wildlifeThe 2015 study titled Marsh rabbit mortalities tie pythons to the precipitous decline of mammals in the Everglades identified Burmese pythons as the dominant cause of mortality among the introduced rabbits in the park. Its authors also argued that python predation could help explain declines among less fecund, or slower-breeding, mammalian prey species, including raccoons, round-tailed muskrats and bobcats. Those species were not directly tested in the rabbit experiment, so the findings do not establish the cause of every mammal decline in the Everglades. Mammals play several ecological roles: they serve as prey and predators, cycle nutrients, and influence vegetation. The researchers warned that their disappearance could affect food-web relationships and ecosystem functioning across the Greater Everglades.

articles.title: Elon Musk has a six-word reply for CEO of America's largest mobile network company who said SpaceX needs eight years to build a rival network
articles.summary: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman thinks SpaceX has a long way to go if it wants to compete with America's big mobile carriers.
articles.body: Verizon CEO Dan Schulman thinks SpaceX has a long way to go if it wants to compete with America's big mobile carriers. On Verizon's third-quarter earnings call on Monday, he said SpaceX would need $300 billion to $500 billion, up to 80,000 cell towers and as long as eight years to build a network that could match Verizon's. Elon Musk replied quickly. "Will take 2 or 3 years," the SpaceX CEO posted on X after the call.The exchange comes at a tense time for US telecom companies. Earlier this month, SpaceX bought low-band spectrum in a deal worth about $8 billion. These airwaves work well for phones, and the news sent Verizon's shares down nearly 9% in one day, the stock's worst day since 2002. SpaceX is also reportedly working to secure at least 80,000 cell sites across the US, and it has approached tower owners including Crown Castle.Verizon CEO says Starlink satellites can't compete in citiesSchulman did not dismiss Musk. He said he works on the assumption that SpaceX will do everything it says it will do, and "execute flawlessly". His argument was that satellites alone cannot match a ground network in cities and suburbs, which account for about 98% of Verizon's revenue. "We're somewhere between 100 to 1000 times more efficient than they are," he said.To close that gap, Schulman said, SpaceX would need 65,000 to 80,000 large tower sites, along with backhaul, radio equipment and more spectrum. He estimated the build would take at least four to six years, with spending spread over seven or eight. Retail stores, customer service and back-office systems would come after that."There is no magic wand. There is no shortcut," he said.Starlink Mobile would be the sixth player in US wireless, not the fourthSchulman added that even a finished network would make SpaceX the sixth competitor in the US market, not the fourth. Verizon's network already carries Spectrum Mobile and Xfinity Mobile, two large cable-backed operators. He also ruled out renting Verizon's network to SpaceX through a wholesale deal, saying he sees no benefit in offering one to a satellite provider."It's very hard to throw a punch against something that doesn't exist. But once they come into the market, we will be ferociously competitive," he said.SpaceX plans to switch on Starlink Mobile in early 2028, using next-generation satellites, ground towers and small home cells. Last week, Musk told investors that Starlink connectivity could eventually bring in several hundred billion dollars a year.Verizon is not the only carrier playing down the threat. Last week, AT&T CEO John Stankey said he "wouldn't over-rotate" on one carrier's low-band spectrum.Verizon's own quarter was strong. The company added 406,000 postpaid phone customers and raised its full-year earnings forecast.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
