articles.title: The world's climate bill is mounting. But who should really foot the cost?
articles.summary: Europe grew rich burning fossil fuels. India is still trying to catch up.
articles.body: Europe grew rich burning fossil fuels. India is still trying to catch up. And when climate disasters strike poorer countries, the bill often lands on those least able to pay.What would you do if someone spent two centuries getting rich by polluting the atmosphere, then handed you a bill for cleaning it up? That, in essence, is the question Commerce minister Piyush Goyal put to Europe in Berlin. His argument was blunt: Countries that industrialised early should not expect developing economies to bear the same costs of tackling climate change.In Nepal, communities were still counting the cost of a devastating flood triggered by a collapse of rock and glacier ice on August 26. Thousands were dead or missing. Bridges, roads and hydropower projects lay damaged. Nepal estimated that recovery and reconstruction would cost $4.71 billion, even though its contribution to global emissions has been tiny.So who pays? Is it the United States and Europe, which grew wealthy while burning coal and oil? Is it China and India, whose emissions now matter enormously to the future of the planet? Or should countries such as Nepal receive help simply because they cannot afford to recover from disasters of this scale?Europe's climate bill comes dueSpeaking at the Berlin Global Dialogue on October 22, Goyal challenged European participants over the continent's historical emissions and its demands for faster climate action from developing countries."The problem was caused by you," he said, arguing that wealthy economies had benefited from cheap fossil fuels while the consequences were increasingly falling on poorer countries.His complaint was also about trade. Since January 1, the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) has entered its definitive phase. It requires importers to account for emissions embedded in certain goods, including steel, aluminium, cement and fertilisers.The EU says the measure prevents companies from moving production to countries with weaker climate rules to avoid paying a carbon price. Goyal sees a different problem: Indian manufacturers could face additional costs while competing against European producers with greater resources to invest in cleaner technology.He also questioned whether wealthy countries had delivered the financial support they promised developing economies. His argument was that asking poorer countries to decarbonise faster makes little sense if they cannot afford the technology needed to do so.There is a serious question here. Can a climate policy be fair if the same rules impose very different costs on countries with vastly different incomes and industrial capabilities?A mountain collapses, and the bill runs into billionsOn August 26, a huge mass of rock and glacier ice collapsed from Langtang Lirung near the Nepal-China border. The debris triggered a devastating flood along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river systems. According to Nepal's disaster authorities, 1,455 people had died and 5,285 remained missing by October 5.The disaster caused an estimated $2.7 billion in damage and economic losses. Recovery and reconstruction needs were put at roughly $4.71 billion.Did climate change cause the collapse? A scientific assessment by World Weather Attribution, published on September 17, offered a more careful answer. Warming was a destabilising factor, likely weakening the rock wall as temperatures rose and ice within fractures thawed. Geology and the region's history of earthquakes also mattered.Not every disaster can be attributed solely to climate change. But a warming climate can increase the risks faced by communities that have little capacity to move away from dangerous terrain or rebuild after a catastrophe.On October 22, the UN's Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage provisionally set aside $21.6 million for Nepal. The sum includes $20 million for potential assistance and $1.6 million in oversight fees. Nepal must still submit a funding request for consideration by the fund's board.Even if the assistance goes ahead, it will cover less than 0.5 per cent of Nepal's estimated recovery bill. The country now faces an uncomfortable choice: find the money elsewhere, borrow more or leave some of the damage unrepaired.Speaking to TOI, Prof Raghu Murtugudde said climate finance remains inadequate, with countries and institutions blurring the distinction between funding for climate-related losses and development projects. “If Nepal is getting $20 million for the damage it has experienced, that's a ridiculously small number. All the loss and damage funds and other climate funds, and even the World Bank, shouldn't be mixing adaptation projects with development projects and calling it climate funding. So, everybody is playing some games,” he said.The historical numbers are hard to ignoreA Carbon Brief analysis published on January 8, estimated that the United States had emitted 542 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide since 1850, accounting for more than a fifth of the global cumulative total under its methodology. China ranked second with 336 billion tonnes. The 27 EU member states together accounted for about 12 per cent.These figures include emissions from fossil fuels, cement and land-use change. They also help explain why historical responsibility matters. Carbon dioxide does not disappear when a factory closes or a power station switches off. A substantial share of the gas released decades ago continues to contribute to global warming.Britain's colonial history adds another dimension. A Carbon Brief analysis published in November 2023 estimated that the UK's share of historical emissions rose from about 3 per cent to 5.1 per cent when emissions associated with 46 former colonies were attributed to British rule. India accounted for the largest share of those additional emissions.Countries that industrialised early enjoyed the benefits of fossil-fuel-powered growth for generations. Many developing countries are now being asked to modernise their economies under tighter carbon constraints.But there is another side to the bill. China's emissions have surged alongside its rise as an industrial powerhouse. India is also among the world's largest annual emitters. The past explains why countries have different responsibilities, but it cannot make today's emissions irrelevant.India's case is strong, but it’s not that simpleGoyal said India represents about 17 per cent of the world's population but contributes less than 3 per cent of global carbon emissions. That figure needs context.According to Our World in Data, using the Global Carbon Budget 2025, India accounted for about 8.27 per cent of global fossil-fuel and industrial carbon dioxide emissions in 2024. It was the world's third-largest emitter by this measure, behind China and the United States.The per-person comparison, however, supports much of India's argument. In 2024, fossil-fuel and industrial CO₂ emissions averaged 2.2 tonnes per person in India, compared with 5.39 tonnes in the EU and 14.2 tonnes in the US. The average EU resident therefore accounted for about 2.45 times India's per-person emissions under this measure.These figures exclude emissions from land-use change. They also measure emissions produced within national borders, rather than adjusting for emissions embedded in traded goods.India's large population means its total emissions are substantial, even though its average person emits far less carbon than the average American or European.Researchers have tried to calculate the debtCan historical responsibility be translated into money? Researchers have attempted exactly that.A 2023 study in Nature Sustainability by Andrew Fanning and Jason Hickel, titled Compensation for atmospheric appropriation, developed a model to calculate what countries that had exceeded their fair share of the carbon budget might owe those that had stayed within theirs.The study tracked emissions across 168 countries from 1960 and modelled a scenario in which all countries reached net zero by 2050. Even under that ambitious scenario, the researchers found that wealthy countries in the Global North would collectively use three times their fair share of the remaining 1.5°C carbon budget.Their model estimated that compensation owed to countries in the Global South could reach $192 trillion by 2050, with average annual payments of about $940 per person across recipient countries.While that is an extraordinary figure, it is also important to understand what it is not. It is not a bill recognised by governments or an amount countries have agreed to pay. It is a model based on assumptions about a fair distribution of the carbon budget and the cost of excess emissions.Still, the research asks an uncomfortable question: Should countries that have used more than their fair share of the atmosphere's limited capacity to absorb carbon help finance the transition of countries that have used less?Murtugudde said that while the need for climate finance is clear, there is little clarity on how the required funding will be mobilised. “The numbers are there: we need a trillion dollars per year by 2035. But where will this money come from? That's not clear,” he said.The International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 2025 added a legal dimension. The court examined states' obligations under international law and the potential consequences of breaching them, including reparation where the legal requirements are met. It did not order countries to pay a fixed amount or establish an automatic right to compensation after every climate disaster. But it gave vulnerable countries a more substantial legal basis for pursuing their claims.Promises are not the same as money in the bankGoyal also criticised wealthy countries over their pledge to provide $100 billion in annual climate finance to developing countries.There is an important correction to his claim that the money never arrived. The target, agreed in 2009 for delivery by 2020, was missed by its original deadline. But OECD figures published on May 21, 2026 show that developed countries provided and mobilised $132.8 billion in 2023 and $136.7 billion in 2024. The $100 billion target was first exceeded in 2022.The argument, therefore, is not that no money has been provided. It is whether the funding is sufficient, accessible and affordable.Much climate finance comes in the form of loans, which must be repaid. Loans can finance useful projects, but they can also increase the burden on countries already struggling with debt. A country that has to borrow to build flood defences and then borrow again to rebuild after a disaster faces a difficult cycle.At COP29 in November 2024, countries agreed to a new goal of at least $300 billion a year in climate finance for developing countries by 2035, with developed countries taking the lead. They also called for efforts to scale up finance from all sources to $1.3 trillion annually by 2035.Prof Murtugudde said that addressing climate change requires international cooperation in funding, knowledge and technology sharing, while countries must also take responsibility for their own development choices. “Everybody has to work together to develop not just funding but also knowledge, expertise, technology sharing, etc., so that developing countries are also helped in dealing with climate impacts. But countries like Nepal are building everywhere in the mountains, so they are making themselves vulnerable too. We have to be responsible for our own actions as well,” he said. “It's a complex issue. The negotiations are complex, but everybody makes statements to position themselves for the negotiations.”The challenge is turning these targets into money that reaches vulnerable communities quickly, rather than leaving them waiting while homes, roads and livelihoods remain in ruins.So who should pay?The climate debate often gets stuck on a familiar argument: Who polluted more, who is developing faster and who should sacrifice what. But for a country like Nepal, the consequences are not theoretical. A destroyed bridge cannot be rebuilt with a historical emissions chart. A family that has lost its home cannot wait for the next climate summit to settle a dispute over responsibility.Europe cannot escape its historical role in creating the crisis. India cannot ignore the weight of its emissions today. And countries such as Nepal cannot be expected to shoulder a multibillion-dollar recovery bill largely on their own. Climate justice will mean little if it asks vulnerable countries to prove, disaster after disaster, that they deserve help.Goyal's challenge to Europe is therefore only part of the argument. The harder test is whether countries that demand accountability are prepared to accept it themselves. The atmosphere may not distinguish between a tonne of carbon emitted in London, Beijing or Delhi. But a fair climate deal must distinguish between those who can afford to pay, those who helped create the problem and those who are already paying for it.

articles.summary: Retired Rear Adm. Tim Gallaudet tells Sean Hannity why the deep ocean's vast unexplored depths could be the ultimate UAP hiding place today.
articles.body: A retired Navy rear admiral is pulling back the curtain on what he believes is an 80-year government UFO cover-up, explaining why the deep ocean could be the ultimate hiding place for unidentified anomalous phenomena (UAPs). "If they were to go somewhere basically to not be detected for a period of time ... where would you want to go?" retired Rear Adm. Tim Gallaudet asked Sean Hannity on his "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "You'd want to go ... [to] the most unexplored area of the world, and that's the ocean." RETIRED NAVY ADMIRAL MAKES BOMBSHELL CLAIM ABOUT UFOS AND 'NON-HUMAN INTELLIGENCE' CONTROLLING THEM Gallaudet, a former acting administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), appeared on Tuesday's episode of the podcast discussing the mysteries of the deep ocean and what could lurk beneath the surface. His decades of experience studying the ocean have led him to question what its depths could contain, particularly given how much of the seafloor remains unmapped, according to ocean-mapping researchers. HARVARD ASTRONOMER TAPPED TO LEAD WHITE HOUSE UFO COUNCIL SAYS US GOVERNMENT 'BAFFLED BY WHAT THEY ARE SEEING' "We've only explored with either drones, buoys, floats, about 10% of ocean volume," Gallaudet said. "So there's a lot of mystery out there right now." His remarks come as Navy personnel have reported encounters with unidentified objects that they say can travel between air and water without any apparent disturbance. Gallaudet described a video that he said shows a mysterious object moving rapidly underwater before emerging from the water without disturbing the surface, hovering briefly and then accelerating skyward. "It goes into the ocean, no disturbance," Gallaudet said. articles.title: Ford Fathom will be the cheapest American EV capable of powering a house | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Ford is rolling out two new chargers capable of powering a home or the grid — so-called V2X capability.
articles.body:
Ford announced two new EV chargers today that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid.

The new chargers promise to be about half the cost of Ford’s existing equivalent products , which could make the technology available to more households. Ford said the Fathom itself will start at $28,350.

The Fathom will be capable of delivering “over 10 kW” to a home, Ford said. That would allow the electric vehicle to substitute for a small standby generator. For most U.S. homes, it wouldn’t be enough to power everything, but it could keep a refrigerator and air conditioner operational for about half a day.

Such capability has been touted as an advantage EVs have over fossil fuel vehicles, but not many EVs come properly equipped, and the chargers required to make use of vehicle-to-everything (V2X) services tend to be costly.

Ford’s two devices offer similar but differing capabilities.

The Home Power Station device can help customers shave their utility bill by charging the Fathom when power prices are low and sending electricity back to the home when prices are high. The automaker says it will cost around $650, about 50% less than its first-generation bidirectional charger.

The other option, Home Backup Power, is a package that bundles the Home Power Station with a second device, the Home Backup Panel, to allow the Fathom to also power parts or all of a home when the power goes out. Ford says the package will cost around $2,100, about 60% less than its first-generation product.

None of those prices include installation, which for existing V2X chargers can run up to $10,000, depending on how much electrical work needs to be done to prepare the home. Ford did not announce any partnerships with installers, though a spokesperson told TechCrunch that Ford would release more details at a later date.

Which loads the Fathom can power will vary by household and the specifics of each installation. Things like air conditioners and refrigerators, for example, typically require a large surge of power to start up, after which point their load drops. So-called soft-start devices can help mitigate the surge, though they add cost to the installation.

Both chargers will allow Fathom customers to participate in virtual power plants (VPPs), which use software to control a fleet of distributed energy storage devices, such as EVs.

As strain on the grid grows due to AI data centers, utilities have been exploring whether VPPs can help alleviate congestion at the edges.

Fathom owners who enroll and keep their truck plugged in can sell electricity back to the grid, often at a premium. Ford did not say how much Fathom owners can stand to make, but the payouts can be upwards of $1,000 per year, depending on the grid’s needs and the level of participation.

Automakers, including Ford , have been diving deep into energy storage as demand for such services surges. The Fathom-powered VPP is Ford’s latest foray into the market, but it’s unlikely to be its last.

articles.title: In Bolivia, a cat mistaken for an ordinary tiger cat for years was recognised as a new species after DNA analysis placed it on a branch split 1.4 million years ago
articles.summary: A groundbreaking genomic analysis reveals Leopardus tilcayo, a new cat species from Bolivia's Yungas forests, marking the first new living cat species description in over a century. Discover its unique features and conservation implications.
articles.body: A small wild cat from Bolivia’s Yungas forests has been formally recognised as a distinct species after genomic analysis revealed an evolutionary lineage separate from other tiger cats. Named Leopardus tilcayo, it is the first newly described living cat species in over a century. This comes from a research paper titled “Phylogenomics and museomics reveal five distinct species of tiger cats in South America”, led by Jonas Lescroart, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz and colleagues. Researchers established the Bolivian animal as a separate species, and they revised the classification of the wider tiger cat group. The paper also places the Bolivian animal within a broader revision of the tiger cat complex, which the authors resolve into five species. Drawing on genomes from museum specimens alongside newly collected samples, they separate the lineage from its closest relatives, and reports describe the cat as about 46 cm long with notably large rosettes.Genome analysis revealed a separate evolutionary lineageThe discovery began with a kitten found on a road near Bolivia’s Yungas forest. As National Geographic reported, the man who found it initially was under the impression that it was a domestic cat and took it home. The animal, which was small even by domestic-cat standards, was later taken to Senda Verde wildlife refuge, where it was nicknamed Tigrino.When Bolivian biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz first examined it, she considered it a tiger cat already known to the scientific world. However, a difference became apparent in 2019, while Nogales-Ascarrunz was preparing a guide to Bolivia’s cats. When comparing her photographs with a reference image of a tiger cat from Brazil, she noticed that Tigrino’s rosettes were much larger and its appearance raised questions, but coat markings alone could not establish whether it belonged to a separate species.The uncertainty was addressed through genomic analysis by Lescroart and colleagues, who analysed complete genomes from 38 individuals in the Neotropical cat genus Leopardus. The dataset included 26 individuals representing different evolutionary units within the disputed tiger cat complex. Eight genomes came from historical museum specimens, which allowed the researchers to obtain genetic evidence from the Guiana Shield, the type locality associated with Leopardus tigrinus.The study combined newly generated genome data with previously published genomes to compare relationships among the cats. Its results placed the Bolivian Yungas lineage apart from its closest tiger cat relatives, with an estimated divergence of approximately 1.4 million years. The name “tilcayo” reflected the local term for the cat, which she told the outlet had been passed down from the residents’ grandfathers.The revised classification raises new conservation questionsAs the Current Biology paper lays out, the research settles how scientists should classify South American tiger cats. Rather than treating the group as one catch-all species, the study identifies five: Leopardus guttulus, L. pardinoides, L. tigrinus, L. emiliae, and the newly described L. tilcayo. They also identified the Peruvian Yungas population as a distinct subspecies, called Leopardus tigrinus antisuyo.The physical differences also help distinguish L. tilcayo from its closest relatives. According to Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz in Guinness World Records, compared with the clouded tiger cat (L. pardinoides), the Bolivian species has shorter fur, a less contrasting coat pattern, more expanded and irregular open rosettes, and a less bushy tail. It also lacks the broad, complete bands found on the other cat’s tail. When compared to L. tigrinus, L. tilcayo has larger, more varied markings and a relatively longer tail, and its genetic differences are even more conclusive.The distinction matters because animals previously grouped under one species name may have different distributions and conservation needs. Taxonomy was necessary because assessments applied to a broad species complex could obscure individual populations’ status and misdirect conservation priorities for management. In terms of its habitat, the Yungas is the only region currently identified as the species’ home, but it doesn’t imply the full extent of its range or how many individuals live there. Since small wild cats can be difficult to identify because they are elusive and closely resemble one another, camera traps were deployed in the forest to help establish where exactly the cat roams outside the sanctuary area.

articles.title: In 2025, a West Virginia student found microplastics in fish from seven Appalachian streams; 55 samples held nearly 2,200 pieces, with particle counts linked to agricultural land use
articles.summary: A groundbreaking study from West Virginia University uncovers widespread microplastic pollution in freshwater fish, highlighting agricultural practices and sewage as significant contributors to environmental contamination across seven Appalachian streams.
articles.body: A study led by West Virginia University undergraduate Isabella Tuzzio in 2025 documented 2,185 microplastic particles in 55 juvenile northern hogsucker fish collected from seven streams in North Central Appalachia. According to the research paper published on 26 March 2025, every fish examined contained particles. The findings provide evidence of widespread contamination in the region’s freshwater ecosystems, which are studied less for microplastics than marine environments. The paper, titled “Widespread Microplastic Pollution in Central Appalachian Streams: Implications for Freshwater Ecosystem Sustainability”, examined fish from nine sampling sites across seven streams (some had multiple sites) within the Cheat, Monongahela, and Ohio River watersheds.Agricultural land use emerged as a key associationThe study identified fibres as the dominant particle form, accounting for 96.61% of all microplastics recorded, while sheets made up 2.01%, foams 0.91% and fragments 0.46%. The particles measured between 0.04 millimetres and 4.77 millimetres in length, with a mean of 0.71 millimetres, according to the paper.Contamination varied by location; for instance, fish from the Cheat River watershed contained an average of 62.09 particles each, when compared to 29.77 in the Monongahela watershed and 19.47 in the Ohio River watershed. The downstream sampling site at Big Sandy Creek recorded the highest site-level average, at 116.22 particles per fish. The researchers also reported that a fish from Big Sandy Creek contained 274 particles, the largest individual count in the sample.In statistical modelling, the proportion of agricultural land in a watershed was positively associated with the number of particles found in fish. A second model also included E. coli levels, which were positively associated with particle counts, although that relationship was not statistically significant. The researchers found agricultural land use was significantly associated with particle counts, while sewage input appeared to be a possible contributor, and they noted that atmospheric deposition could not be ruled out. The researchers also found a significant relationship between fish length and particle counts. Larger northern hogsuckers tended to contain more microplastics, although fish size did not significantly predict the average length of individual particles. They cautioned that the limited size range, from 5.6 to 12.8 centimetres, warranted further investigation.The study highlights gaps in freshwater researchAccording to WVU Today’s report, Tuzzio identified synthetic laundry fibres, the study’s dominant form, and face-wash beads as everyday sources of microplastics. The report also raised concerns about particles carrying chemicals, heavy metals, and antibiotics through ecosystems. The research team recommended further work involving other fish species and the possible role of precipitation and atmospheric deposits in moving microplastics through ecosystems. Tuzzio also told WVU Today that public awareness and practical changes could form part of responses, including recycling, environmentally friendlier detergents, washing-machine filters and improvements to waste management and water treatment infrastructure.The northern hogsucker was selected because it is a bottom-dwelling fish native to the region and primarily fed on material found on streambeds. The species was also used as an indicator of stream condition because of its sensitivity to pollution. After the specimens had been preserved for an earlier, separate ecological project, researchers examined the fish’s gastrointestinal tracts.The samples were suspended in a 10% potassium hydroxide solution for 72 hours at 40°C before filtering and inspecting the particles under a dissecting microscope. Moreover, procedural controls were implemented to estimate contamination introduced during laboratory work. Those controls contained 498 particles in total, an average of 9.05 per control. The study’s central finding remained specific: all 55 sampled northern hogsuckers contained microplastics, while the distribution of particles differed between sites and was tied to agricultural land cover.
